articles.title: Rockstar workers vote on union recognition as GTA VI launch looms
articles.description: UK staff get their say while a separate union-busting dispute heads towards its conclusion
articles.content:
More than 1,600 Rockstar Games employees in the UK will begin voting on union recognition on Thursday, with the ballot kicking off just a week before the long-awaited launch of Grand Theft Auto VI.

The ballot, which opens on November 12 and runs until November 26, will determine whether Rockstar formally recognizes the Rockstar Game Workers Union, part of the Independent Workers Union of Great Britain (IWGB). Nearly all UK employees below director level are eligible to vote.

If successful, the union would become the largest recognized union in the UK games industry, giving workers a collective voice.

The proposed recognition agreement follows four months of negotiations between Rockstar management and employees. It would allow workers to negotiate over pay, overtime, pensions, bonuses, leave and other employment conditions, while securing consultation rights over HR policies and AI.

The vote comes at a particularly busy time for Rockstar, with GTA VI finally due to arrive on November 19, more than 13 years after its predecessor. The game is expected to be one of the biggest entertainment launches in history, although the people responsible for making it have rather more immediate concerns than sales records.

"I am incredibly proud of the work we've put into making this game. I'm also proud of the union we've built here. For me, those two things are connected," said Nestor Uriate, an animation programmer and Rockstar Game Workers Union representative.

"We care deeply about the games we make, and we want to make sure we can continue doing that work in an environment where we're respected, have a meaningful say over our conditions and can feel secure about our futures."

The vote follows a year of bad blood between Rockstar and the IWGB. The union accused the GTA developer of union busting after it fired 31 members in October 2025, claiming they had been singled out for taking part in a private Discord group.

Rockstar denied the allegations, insisting the workers were dismissed for gross misconduct rather than their union activities.

The dispute subsequently reached an employment tribunal, where Rockstar unsuccessfully attempted to have blacklisting allegations struck from the case. Closing submissions are expected on November 17 and 18, meaning the legal proceedings will reach their final stages just as GTA VI prepares to hit shelves.

Despite the ongoing dispute, Rockstar's head of publishing, Jennifer Kolbe, recently indicated that management would respect the outcome of the recognition vote, telling Bloomberg: "We go where the team goes. So if they want a union, they will have a union."

The union campaign has also attracted support from elsewhere in the games industry, including SAG-AFTRA and the Communications Workers of America (CWA), which represents workers at Blizzard.

Alex Marshall, president of the IWGB, said the vote was an opportunity for Rockstar employees to take greater control over their working conditions.

"What happens at Rockstar matters beyond the studio. Workers across the games industry are watching, and this ballot is an opportunity to show what can be achieved when people come together, organize and build the collective power to shape their own working lives."

For Rockstar, November was already shaping up to be a big month. By the time GTA VI has been in players' hands for a week, the company should also know whether its UK workforce has voted to secure a formal seat at the negotiating table. ®

articles.title: Google reworks TPU silicon into specialized systems for agents and security
articles.description: Google’s TPU 8i Max and TPU 8tx reuse TPU 8i and TPU 8t silicon to target long-context agents and confidential inference.
articles.content:
Google's eighth-generation TPU family has now expanded further. Back in April, the company announced TPU 8t for training AI models and TPU 8i for general-purpose inference workloads. Google has now introduced TPU 8tx, built on the same silicon as the previously announced 8t, for confidential, hardware-isolated inference aimed at regulated enterprises and governments, and TPU 8i Max, which combines two 8i chips on one package for long-context agentic work.

TPU 8tx swaps the Arm-based Axion hosts of the 8t and 8i for a 5th Gen AMD EPYC CPU, adopting a Boardfly network, and the 8i Max doubles the compute, SRAM, and HBM bandwidth of the original 8i. The original split, the TPU 8t and 8i, made natural sense. The 8t targets large-scale training, while the 8i leans toward low-latency inference and reasoning. TPUs have become a fast-growing business, with the company claiming nearly 100 customers, including Meta’s recent move to TPUs. The more modular approach is flexible and can deliver specialized systems “in a matter of months rather than years,” helping that popularity along.

For the new parts, the TPU 8i Max isn't innovative on the surface, as it’s just two TPU 8i chips combined into a single package. The result is twice the theoretical compute, but more importantly, it fits twice the silicon within the “existing rack footprint,” and Google claims more compute per square foot and per watt.

Doubling both SRAM and HBM bandwidth helps keep things scaling, which would put the 8i Max at about 20.2 FP4 PFLOPS, 768 MB SRAM, and about 17.2 TB/s HBM bandwidth. This compares to Nvidia’s Rubin R200 GPU at a rated 50 FP4 PFLOPS for inference and 22 TB/s of HBM4 per socket, or AMD’s MI455X with 40 FP4 PFLOPS. The compute gap is closing.

The memory bandwidth doubling is also potentially one way around moving to HBM4. The memory wall, as Google calls it, or the bandwidth bottleneck, is a real concern “when dozens of AI agents work together across an entire software codebase.” Larger context windows — with larger models targeting 1 million tokens — mean larger KV caches, partly held in SRAM, and each new token has to read that cache back from memory, which is where the extra HBM bandwidth helps. It’s a different route from Nvidia’s LPX: more bandwidth in one package, rather than a second chip type for decoding and a storage tier for context.

Google also provides useful software for agents to get the most out of its hardware. TPU Sync is an open-source “model-state layer for TPU clusters” that moves KV caches off the chip’s HBM, “automatically tiering massive KV caches off the chip in milliseconds” down to host DRAM and, experimentally, shared storage. Google says this can cut KV transfer latency by “more than 90%,” with time-to-first-token gains that vary by workload. The company has also announced the Agent Compute Engine, a Google Cloud service that pauses idle agent sessions and moves their working memory aside until they’re needed again, another memory-saving effort.

Google credits its vLLM-TorchTPU stack with “state-of-the-art price-performance marks” on InferenceX and AgentX, which test realistic agentic coding and long-context work. However, the only published third-party numbers so far are for the last-generation Ironwood TPU. In SemiAnalysis ’s InferenceX tests in September, running Qwen3.5 397B in FP8, Ironwood delivered 50.4% more tokens per dollar than Nvidia’s B200 and 96.0% more than the B300 at 20 tokens per second per user. One issue with that, however, is that Ironwood lacks native FP4, although newer November results show its FP8 beating Nvidia’s FP4 GB300 NVL72 on the same model, at 1.67 times the performance per dollar. There is also no eighth-gen result yet to compare how the new generation differs.

In contrast to the 8i Max, which is designed for long-context work, the new TPU 8tx, “built on the same silicon as TPU 8t,” is “optimized for secure and confidential inference” as well as small-scale training. The security is built into the hardware with isolation to prevent snooping on sensitive data, including model weights. Normally, data has to be unlocked in memory during processing, which is the step this isolation is meant to cover.

This chip is intended for areas where security and confidentiality are high priorities, which means regulated enterprises and governments, particularly those who are using frontier or proprietary models. In that case, the operators may want to “fine-tune models using their private data, distill large models into smaller ones, and train their agents,” without having to move sensitive data between clusters. Agents and security meet here for “secure agent execution.” Back in April, the Pentagon and Google reportedly held discussions for TPU usage in classified settings, although the 8tx chip is not specifically named.

Google’s Private AI Compute, its “hardened TPU platform” with protections “comparable to a typical TEE,” per its September technical brief, already runs confidential serving on TPUs. The 8tx appears to be that capability turned into a product for customers. Alternatives include Nvidia’s NVL72, with one security domain across 72 Rubin GPUs, 36 Vera CPUs, and the interconnects, and Intel’s TDX, which is adding trusted I/O to cover data moving to accelerators.

The TPU 8tx hosts are based on 5th Gen AMD EPYC boards, instead of the Axion hosts on the 8t, which replaced x86 in April. There's one Axion for every two TPUs on the 8i, compared with one Xeon per four on Ironwood. Google gives no reason for the change, but its Confidential VM configuration list has both AMD and Intel series chips, with no Arm-based ones listed. Private AI Compute uses “an AMD-based hardware Trusted Execution Environment” for its CPU workloads, suggesting Google swapped something it already runs on its confidential stack.

The 8tx also adopts the 8i’s Boardfly network over the 8t’s torus, which Google claims can deliver “up to 2x lower latency compared to TPU 8t” with almost no performance penalty, although it’s not clear what measure Google is using. The alternative torus network suits training, since chips mostly swap data with neighbors in a predictable manner, but inference on large mixture-of-experts and reasoning models can send smaller messages between distant chips, with every hop adding delay. With Boardfly, it’s at most seven hops against 16 at 1,024 chips.

What is lacking is a full specifications table, the amount of HBM capacity, pod sizes, an availability date, pricing, and customers for either system. Details on attestation, that is, the ability for the customer to verify confidentiality, are also missing for 8tx. The 8tx and 8i Max are currently listed, along with the 8i and 8t, as “coming soon” on Google’s Cloud TPU page.

Delivering two new TPU systems nearly seven months after April’s pair shows Google wants to turn out specialized systems much more quickly than has been the case in the past. Now, it just needs to prove them, through benchmarks and an availability date when the hardware is actually in customers’ hands.

articles.title: Techie uses voltage glitching hack to turn $2,500 Nvidia 8GB cryptomining GPU into a full-fat $20,000 A100 with 80GB of VRAM
articles.description: A techie turned a $2,500 CMP-170HX 8GB mining card into a full-fat $20,000 A100 80GB by carefully blowing onboard fuses to unlock entire VRAM and shader modules.
articles.content:
Enterprising techies looking to build their own local AI cluster have far more interesting options than buying DGX Sparks or Apple Mac Studios. Used data center GPUs are everywhere, and a server rack's garbage is an enthusiast's treasure. This option has become even more popular with CMPunlocker, a soft-mod for Nvidia CMP-170HX cards that unlocks abilities well beyond stock. Now, a techie has taken it a step further, blasting through the remaining limitations with voltage glitching and creating a card faster than the actual $20,000 Nvidia A100 GPU with 80GB of VRAM... but from an $2,500 8GB CMP-170HX mining card.

The volt-mod was done by Kate ( GitHub link here ), who got her starting point from a paper that described how one could exploit GA100 cards' microcode. She turned her attention to the normally protected onboard fuse controller. Although it's rarely discussed, a "fuse box" has been integral in most any CPU and GPU for a while — though it's normally used once at the factory to break physical connections in chips to parts that have tested poorly, thus disabling them so they can be sold as a lower-end model.

If you're wondering how people are getting 80-40GB of VRAM out of 8-10GB, the explanation is simple: the GA100 silicon actually includes all the corresponding HBM2e VRAM dies within; but they get disabled at the factory like the shader modules. The smaller version is more desirable, as it's based on the variant of GA100 with 80GB of HBM2e within, while the 10GB cards spawn from the 40GB GA100.

The Nvidia cards in question have quite an elaborate eFuse controller (16,384 in a 512 x 32 array) — which can be read to obtain the card's current configuration. Most every part of the card has related fuses: VRAM sections, individual shader modules, PCIe 4.0 and NVLink, and even video codec hardware. However, as Kate succinctly put it: Nvidia's design is insecure, as popping fuses can grant access to more features, not fewer.

Under normal conditions, these fuses can't be popped, or "written to," by the user — but a geek armed with a soldering iron isn't a normal user. Kate had GPT-6 Astra design a simple circuit board based on an $8 STM32G4 microcontroller to tap into the power signals on the card's PCB.

The voltage regulators (VRMs) on the card "speak" PWMVID, an Nvidia standard, and Kate's board intercepted the PWM signals sent into the VRM controller, forcing it to produce voltage glitches on the line feeding the GPU, where the fuse controller lies.

Remember when we said the fuse controller was read-only? With the voltage glitches, many fuse-status reads in a tight loop, and she managed to set the controller to a state in which its security bit flags allowed writes through. From that point, it was "easy" to reconfigure her card. She was careful to force-disable any shader modules previously marked as defective, because these are physical fuses — there's no "undo" button.

She applied the mod to her cards and, after testing with multiple workloads, found that nine had the full 80 GB of VRAM working, and one card "only" had 64 GB usable. Most interestingly, unlocking all the shader modules (SM) nets her FP16 FMA performance 20% beyond a regular A100 card. She thinks this is due to the chips often having 120 or more usable SMs — over the 108 on the spec sheet. The GA100 die starts with 128 SMs to account for defects, which is normal in chip manufacturing.

The CMPUnlocker soft mod is required for enabling the "new" features on the drivers, but it doesn't unlock the card's full potential: the VRAM upper limit is 40-64GB (depending on the variant), many shader modules remain locked, and PCIe bandwidth only goes to 2.0. Additionally, there's no ECC, NVLink, or multi-instance GPU support, all of which are critical in a server setup and are also used for product segmentation.

Kate's volt-mod does away with all of these limits, and her best test card is happily working at PCIe 4.0 speed with the full feature set. She didn't test the video encoder bits, but it's unlikely anybody using these cards cares much for that.

As for the cost, a CMP-170HX 8GB is currently hovering around $3,000, and the 10GB variant costs around $2,500. A full-fat Nvidia A100 80GB in a PCIe configuration can reach $20,000 or more. The SXM server-module versions are cheaper, but they require infrastructure around them. Note that these prices will likely vary significantly, especially as people become increasingly aware of the mods.

Kate says she's publishing her research now because another person independently found the same issue. She has informed Nvidia of the vulnerability, though there's not much the company can do for existing cards already on the market.

articles.title: Orbit Global Menu: A working global menu addon for GNOME
articles.description: We love this, but suspect this is the Marmite of GNOME extensions
articles.content:
A new extension brings a working global menu bar to the GNOME desktop, even for some apps that don’t have menu bars at all.

Orbit Global Menu is a new GNOME extension that gives the GNOME desktop a feature it was intentionally designed without, and one that some users miss very badly – this vulture being one of them. It adds a working global menu bar to the GNOME top panel. We suspect this is something that will cause strongly contrasting opinions among many GNOME users: some will by puzzled why anyone would bother, while others may think "at last!" and rush to try it.

There have been other attempts to do this before, and the Reg FOSS desk has tried several of them, but we never found one that worked with the majority of applications. Our fondness for this UI feature was visible in the two-part series we wrote in September on how to customize Xfce and then in part two how to get the global menu working with more apps.

The problem is getting worse over time, as in recent versions (since GNOME 40 and Gtk4), the GNOME human-interface guidelines encourage smartphone-style hamburger menus, replacing the traditional horizontal menu bar. It is tricky to add global menu bar support to apps that lack a menu bar, but Orbit's developer "Unmade" found a rather labor-intensive solution. The menu bar applet contains maps of keyboard controls for 292 different apps, so it can show a menu all on its own and then send those apps simulated keystrokes to operate it. It's not the programs' full menu trees, just a subset of them, but it works.

It's also not the most elegant solution, but it is a solution and it works. We tried it on Ubuntu 26.10 and every app in the full install worked to at least some extent. If you are willing and able to build and install a small additional connector, it lets the global-menu applet talk to lots more applications.

The GNOME shell is unusual among open source desktop environments, to an extent that we have criticized before. GNOME Shell was designed with a distinctive look and feel of its own, unlike almost all other desktops. It has a minimalist, stripped-down layout that doesn't look or work quite like anything else, and it's intentionally not very customizable. To change how GNOME works means writing new Javascript code, then packaging it as an extension that users can install from the GNOME Extensions website. This requires both a browser extension and a "native host messaging" connector to be installed into the underlying OS – or a purpose-written app. By default, the desktop comes with neither.

The end result is that GNOME lends a visual identity to the Linux desktop, one that is clear and distinct from either Windows or macOS. (Back in 2013, this vulture argued that when Microsoft threatened to sue multiple Linux vendors over infringing Windows UI patents, some 20 years ago, this UI fragmentation was just what the company wanted.) GNOME 2 was the Linux world's default desktop. GNOME Shell was controversial in its early days, and lost pole position, but it has since won it back. Today, GNOME is the default desktop on all the major distros: Ubuntu, Fedora and Red Hat Enterprise Linux and the RHELatives, as well as Debian and SUSE, all default to GNOME.

GNOME does away with a lot of features that are significant functional parts of other graphical desktops. For instance, it has no desktop icons, no system tray or defined place for status indicators, and neither GNOME nor GNOME-compliant applications have menu bars, either inside windows (Microsoft style) or in the top panel (Apple macOS style). This is disorienting and confusing for those used to controlling software mainly using their menus – but now, that's mainly older hands. This design suits those who grew up on smartphones and tablets, or who feel more comfortable with their stripped-back keyboardless UI than a full desktop WIMP, which can be overwhelming to newbies and non-techies.

If you've followed the evolution of graphical desktops for some 40 years, as this gray-plumed vulture has, some trends are very apparent that aren't so clear if you came in once evolution was underway.

Apple introduced the first global menu bar in the Lisa, and improved on that in the Macintosh. DR GEM copied it very early on, but Apple sued and DR changed the PC version of GEM to be less Mac-like. Microsoft's Windows came along after this, and moved menu bars inside windows instead. When Apple acquired NeXT in 1996, it moved NeXTstep's patent-avoidant vertical menus back to a global bar at the top, along with the clock and some status indicators. There they remain, 30 years later. In 2007, it launched the iPhone, containing a very cut-down OS based on OS X, replacing the Finder with a cut-down version of the Dashboard layer from OS X 10.4. The panel remained, shorn of its menus, which were too fiddly for a small screen.

As The Register mentioned in 2017, in its preliminary releases, Android started out as a keypad-driven Java phone that looked and worked very much like BlackBerry. When the iPhone appeared, Google changed course. The new Android UI resembled iOS, complete with that top panel, still without menus. GNOME 3.0 was not far behind: in 2009 the team promised a revamp of the user experience, and in 2011, launched GNOME 3.0. It too has the fixed top panel — now huge on a laptop or desktop landscape screen – and mostly empty.

Now that top panel regains its original 1983 function. We're rather impressed by the Orbit global menu. It does the job, and it even works with apps that don't have menu bars. It's not perfect: for instance, over-long menus have to scroll, and may fail to do so if new submenus appear.

The GitHub repository has extensive instructions, including how to build and install the optional connector module that lets more apps export their real menus to the extension. It also tells you how to instruct some apps, notably Firefox, that there is a global menu for it to use. We are saddened to note that, as is so often the case, Wayland gets in the way here.

It works rather well with some other extensions, too. With a menu bar, GNOME's strangely centered clock seems out of place, but several extensions, such as F rippery Move Clock, shove it over to the right where we still feel it belongs. If you prefer a lighter-colored panel and dock, it also plays nicely with Blur my Shell. ®

articles.title: Struggling marijuana farmers pivot to becoming AI data center sites to escape falling weed revenue
articles.description: One expert says that it still depends on the perfect confluence of cheap power, favorable regulation, and reliable connectivity.
articles.content:
The AI data center boom is bringing hope to struggling cannabis farmers as they face increased competition, costs, and taxes amid reduced demand for marijuana. According to Arizona Public Media, the cannabis industry is in decline, with sales peaking in 2024 and oversupply driving prices down. And now, several growers are considering selling their cultivation facilities or converting them into “mini data center nodes.” These facilities already have many of the ingredients needed for AI data centers, such as the increasingly hard-to-get supply of electricity and water infrastructure.

"For some reason, there's a lot more cannabis grown in Arizona than Arizonans use. And so, a lot of folks are getting out of that business, like myself, at least on the cultivation side. But these facilities can potentially be repurposed to be mini data center nodes," Moe Asnani, the former owner of two Tucson D2 Dispensaries, told the public broadcaster. He also added, "The whole idea is if you create these smaller nodes where people control their own data, where they're not at the mercy of other people's updates and things like that — that's kind of where the idea came in, because I believe in decentralization."

Cannabis farming is both power- and water-intensive. Forbes looked at a 32,850-square-foot cannabis facility in Kalamazoo, Michigan, which is currently wired for 1.5 megawatts, which can be expanded to 2.5 megawatts in under a year and 15 megawatts in the long term. It's also provisioned for fiber internet and equipped with a state-of-the-art HVAC system for climate control, which should make it a tempting property for anyone wanting to put up a small data center — something that even OpenAI and Anthropic are interested in as massive hyperscale sites face opposition from the community.

This concept is dubbed "adaptive reuse," with Tucson City Council member Paul Cunningham saying that it’s a more palatable alternative to massive, purpose-built sites sitting on the outskirts of town. "Data centers are dirty words, and everybody knows that. And no one wants to build a brand-new data center anywhere," the politician said. "But if we have buildings that were using that amount of water and that amount of energy already in their previous function and [it] can be done without being invasive, I'm OK with exploring that option."

There is massive demand for data centers, but it’s not a guaranteed payoff for struggling cash-strapped growers looking to unload their unprofitable properties. Niki Krear, vice president of acquisitions of real estate investment trust New Lake Capital Partners, said that there’s a sweet spot between connectivity, costs, and regulation that data center operators look for in a site.

"It’s a combination of finding affordable power, dense fiber networks, and favorable tax policies," Krear told MJBizDaily. Even though many cultivation facilities already boast higher-than-average power capacity for lighting and climate control, data centers often demand twice to thrice more, with upgrades possibly taking up to five years.

Data center operators looking for smaller sites may also have to contend with NIMBY — not in my backyard — fights from neighbors. Additionally, there may be zoning restrictions, moratoriums, and regulatory hurdles, and the lack of economies of scale could end up costing operators more.

This is particularly important as AI chips are expected to increase in power and efficiency in the next five years. As these new AI GPUs become available, data centers will need to sell their existing equipment and buy new hardware to remain competitive. Because suppliers usually offer favorable pricing for larger orders, upgrading these smaller sites will likely end up being more expensive on a per-unit basis. That said, growing opposition toward large new projects could make these former cannabis farms suitable alternatives for operators desperate to get more compute online quickly, provided they check all (or most of) the boxes they need.

articles.title: London hotel put admin login for booking website on whiteboard behind the front desk
articles.description: You could check out more than your room
articles.content:
Welcome, once again, to PWNED, where all the victims are self-owned. This week, we welcome you to a London hotel where you could check out its admin credentials for a booking website just by walking past the front desk.

Our story comes courtesy of Neycho Tepavicharov, co-founder of Flashcloud, a Delaware-based web hosting company. He was staying at a hotel in London when he noticed a shocking breach of basic security protocols by management, who were a little too hospitable with their credentials.

As he was passing through the lobby, Tepavicharov noticed that the door behind the front desk was open and, inside that back room, there was a whiteboard. On the whiteboard, written in plain English, were the hotel’s Booking.com administrative username and password.

Anyone near the desk could clearly see the login information, and if they didn’t have time to write it down, they could have snapped a picture for later use. As Tepavicharov explains, there’s plenty of mischief you could perform with these credentials.

“With that login, someone could change or cancel reservations, see guests’ names and contact details, or message guests pretending to be the hotel,” he said. “Fake 'please confirm your payment' messages sent from compromised hotel accounts are a well-known scam.”

An attacker could potentially exploit that access to disrupt hotel operations or target guests with convincing scams. Whether the exposed credentials alone would have been enough to access the account would depend on its security settings.

Tepavicharov decided to play the role of good samaritan and warn the hotel’s manager that the business was endangering itself by showing everyone its password.

“I asked to speak with the manager and showed him what I’d seen. He was mortified and very grateful,” Tepavicharov said. “Nobody on staff had thought of it as a risk. It was just the easiest way for the whole team to share one login.”

After Tepavicharov talked to the manager, not only did the hotel change its ways, but it also moved its website to his hosting service, Flashcloud.

Tepavicharov notes that there are plenty of takeaways from this incident. Most important: give each user dedicated credentials with their own separate login, and use multi-factor authentication.

“The lesson is an old one, but it keeps happening,” he said. “Shared logins end up written somewhere convenient. Give each staff member their own login, turn on two-factor authentication, and keep passwords in a password manager, not on the wall.” ®

articles.title: Data sovereignty takes more than keeping data close to home
articles.description: SPONSORED POST: Knowing where your data lives is only part of the challenge. Who controls it, who can access it and how quickly you can recover when things go wrong matter just as much.
articles.content:
Keeping sensitive data within national borders might satisfy a residency requirement. But does it mean your organization is genuinely in control?

Not necessarily. Data could be stored locally while remaining subject to another jurisdiction's laws, dependent on overseas service providers or exposed to disruption beyond your control.

For enterprise IT teams, that distinction is becoming harder to ignore. Geopolitical tensions, evolving regulations and the growing use of AI are forcing organizations to reconsider what data sovereignty means in practice. Yet translating those concerns into a workable strategy is another matter.

And simply throwing more money at the problem won't necessarily solve it.

In The Register's on-demand webinar, Data Sovereignty By Design, moderator Tim Phillips speaks with Patrick Smith, Field CTO for EMEA at Everpure, formerly Pure Storage, about moving beyond compliance checklists and taking a more strategic approach to data control.

Drawing on findings from Everpure's research, Smith explores a curious disconnect: organizations are increasing their investment in sovereignty initiatives, yet many still lack a coordinated strategy. Some of the risks attracting the most attention aren't necessarily those receiving the greatest investment.

The discussion examines why sovereignty shouldn't be treated as an IT-only responsibility. Decisions about which data needs protection, which services must remain operational and what level of risk is acceptable require input from business leaders, security, procurement and legal teams.

There's also the question of priorities. Not every workload needs the same sovereign controls, and attempting to protect everything equally can make an already complicated challenge considerably harder.

Smith explains the concept of the "minimum viable company," identifying the critical services, applications and data an organization needs to keep operating through disruption. He also considers why visibility into data access, supplier dependencies and potential exit strategies should influence technology decisions from the outset.

For IT leaders trying to turn sovereignty from an abstract boardroom concern into something actionable, the conversation offers useful questions to take back to their organizations.

Because knowing where your data sits is one thing. Knowing whether you can maintain control when circumstances change is quite another.

articles.title: Your AI agent is only as good as your endpoint data
articles.description: PARTNER CONTENT: Real-time endpoint data keeps AI-driven IT operations accurate, fast and under control
articles.content:
Every so often a flaw comes along that shows how fast the ground can shift under IT and security teams. PHP2Shell, a pair of critical flaws in PHP, was one of them. Details leaked before the planned disclosure, frontier AI helped researchers find the flaws, and PHP shipped fixes the next day. For many teams, though, the patch was the easy part. So what does it take to respond at that speed, and where should teams begin?

What does governed autonomous IT look like in practice?

Picture a loop. Software finds where a risk lives and ranks what matters most. It proposes a fix, then, inside limits people define, carries it out and checks that it worked. Routine, low-risk actions can run on their own. Higher-impact ones wait for a person to approve. A few are never handed over at all. Each step leaves a record that someone can review and reverse.

What challenges do IT and security teams face today?

Three problems keep coming up. The first is visibility. PHP2Shell reportedly sat undetected for more than a decade. For these two flaws, the fix was a version upgrade. The hard part was finding every copy of PHP, including copies bundled inside other software or extracted by hand onto Windows machines that never registered as installed applications. Then teams had to work out which copies the internet could reach and check for signs of earlier attack. An inventory built from a periodic snapshot can't answer those questions on the day they matter.

The second is tool-hopping. Answering "where does this run, and can the internet reach it?" often means pivoting across an asset inventory, a vulnerability scanner and an external attack surface tool, each with its own view. Every hop adds delay. Every console is another chance to disagree with the last.

The third is pace. Several security firms reported exploitation attempts before PHP released its fixes, and Cloudflare reported early attacks hours ahead of the patch. Frontier AI models helped find PHP2Shell, and in April Anthropic said its Claude Mythos Preview model had found thousands of previously unknown flaws across every major operating system and browser. With models like these in the picture, the old rhythm of disclose, patch and verify assumes a gap that keeps shrinking.

Put an AI agent on top of stale, fragmented data and these problems don't go away. They scale.

Why does real-time endpoint data make autonomy trustworthy?

Endpoints are where work happens and where many attacks end up, so they are the ground truth for any decision about the estate. Four qualities make that data a sound foundation for autonomous action:

Accuracy: Live data from the endpoints themselves, not a snapshot that was true last week.

Speed: A short path from question to action, with no hopping between tools to reconcile answers.

Control: Approvals and an audit trail, plus the ability to roll back, so any automated action can be reviewed and reversed.

Shared truth: IT operations, security and the system of record working from one view, rather than arguing over whose data is right.

Matt Psencik, a threat research engineer at Tanium, put the visibility problem bluntly when PHP2Shell broke: "The installations that worry me most are the ones a security team doesn't know it owns."

How does AI fit in?

AI sits on both sides of this. It helped researchers find the PHP2Shell flaws, and attackers can use it to build exploits too. For defenders, AI works best as the operator and the interface: it takes a plain-language question, works out what to ask of the data, and proposes or carries out the next step. But it is only as good as the data it is grounded in. A fluent answer built on outdated information is still wrong, just more confidently so. Keeping people in the loop where stakes are high is what makes automation safe to expand.

What are the practical first steps?

Teams don't need to hand over the keys all at once. Start here:

Find every copy: Don't stop at the installed-applications list. PHP2Shell showed that software bundled inside other products can slip past it. Compare your CMDB against what is really on your network and record exact versions.

Draw the lines: Rank systems by what the internet can reach, then decide which response actions run automatically, which need approval and which are never delegated. Write it down before an agent needs it.

Pilot one low-risk workflow: Pick something contained, build approval into it, and read the audit trail before widening the scope.

Teams can also shorten the pilot with a partner. World Wide Technology (WWT), a Tanium partner, works with many large organizations on technology rollouts and hosts a Tanium lab in its Advanced Technology Center, where customers can test an approach hands-on before moving it into production.

That second problem, the hopping, is the one Tanium Atlas was built to close. Instead of moving between consoles, an operator asks a plain-language question, gets an answer from live endpoint data, and acts on it inside limits the team sets, with every action recorded. articles.title: AWS distills its cloud into a local emulator that runs on your PC
articles.description: Hyperscale meets micro-computing by offering APIs to test your apps
articles.content:
AWS has released an emulator that kind-of-almost lets you use its cloud on a PC.

As explained in the GitHub repository for the prosaically named “AWS Emulator,” the tool “is a local program that serves an AWS API endpoint.”

The emulator doesn’t replicate the whole AWS cloud, instead offering its APIs.

“You use it to test your software without calling AWS, on your own machine, on a development server, or in continuous integration (CI),” the repo explains. Because those tests never touch the AWS cloud, the tool is free to use.

AWS wrote the emulator in Rust, a choice that senior specialist solutions architect Daniel Abib wrote helps to ensure the tool “stays light on CPU and memory on a laptop.”

The emulator tool doesn’t replicate the entire AWS cloud. Abib said it supports the APIs of AWS services that have an API model in the AWS API models repository on GitHub. The Register found over 1,300 items on that page.

While the tool lets developers test APIs, it doesn’t replicate anywhere near all the features of the Amazonian cloud.

“It doesn’t evaluate IAM [Identity and Access Management] policies the way AWS does, and each emulator acts as a single account, with no cross-account or cross-Region behavior,” Abib wrote, adding “How closely it matches AWS varies by service and feature.”

AWS publishes “fidelity scores” that detail how closely the emulator works on different AWS services. Amazon tries to achieve full fidelity, so the emulator produces the same results as AWS for valid API calls, and the same errors for invalid ones.

Coding agents can also drive the Emulator, an option The Register mentions because AWS advises the easiest way to check if a project will work with the tool is to use the aws-emulator skill for AI coding agents.

“With the skill, your agent finds the AWS operations and resources that your project depends on. It checks them against the fidelity tests and fidelity scores for the emulator. It then tells you which parts of your project you can rely on the emulator for, and which ones might behave differently from AWS,” according to AWS documentation.

AWS has made the emulator available as an RPM or Debian package. Mac and PC users will need to run Docker and an image of the Emulator.

“You install the emulator, start it, and point your tools at the local endpoint,” Abib instructed. “When AWS Emulator starts, it generates its own credentials, a config file, and a certificate, and writes them to ~/.aws/emulator/9297/. You set environment variables so the AWS SDK talks to your laptop instead of AWS, and your application code stays unchanged.”

“From there, your existing tests, CLI scripts, and coding agents keep working the way they already do. A unit test that creates an Amazon DynamoDB table, writes an item, and reads it back is the same test, and it runs on your machine without a deployment.”

The cloud colossus’s intent appears, as ever, to encourage more use of its cloud – in this case by satisfying developers their code will run well when deployed there, and making it easy for them to test for that. ®

articles.title: Disgraced former CA eMudhra blames buggy script for hopelessly weak certificates
articles.description: Couldn’t get the hardware it needed to generate certs, so tried to code a workaround
articles.content:
Former certification authority eMudhra has claimed a buggy Python script is the main reason it issued laughably insecure digital certificates.

The company posted its account of the matter on Bugzilla where a user with the handle “Naveen Kumar ML” wrote “During a single key‑generation ceremony on 30 April 2025, sixteen subordinate (issuing) CA key pairs in eMudhra’s ‘B’ and ‘C’ series were generated correctly on a hardware security module and then processed through an approved wrap/unwrap round‑trip using a custom python key‑handling script.”

eMudhra aimed to create eight ECDSA P-384 private keys which should have been 48 bytes long. But the script contained what Kumar described as “a bug/defect in the import code [which] resulted in a read‑back from the unwrapped object that truncated the private value, so the certified public keys correspond to private scalars below the expected range and are recoverable from public information.”

The truncation is the key problem here, because it appears that eMudhra ignored 47 of the 48 bytes, producing its infamously insecure single-byte keys such as the number four.

Whatever the nature of the bug, Kumar asserts it was “a custom script run only on an isolated ceremony host and was not a function of the emCA software.”

eMudhra needed that script because “global supply chain constraints” meant it couldn’t acquire the hardware security modules (HSMs), devices that generate and store cryptographic keys, that it wanted to use when creating a set of certificates for use in the USA.

It therefore used HSMs made by a company called Utimaco to generate keys and planned to transfer the keys it produced to a different set of HSMs from a company called Crypto4A.

Kumar explained that eMudhra decided on that move, which is unusual, because changes to policy about provenance of certificates meant it had to generate new certs by the end of May.

The plan went sour when the company didn’t notice the errors in its script and didn’t test the keys it created.

The rest is history: a Mozilla team member noticed that the company’s keys were woefully weak and pointed out that attackers could therefore issue fraudulent certificates that allowed them to impersonate servers, observe traffic, or even modify data in transit. Browser-makers quickly tweaked their software so it would not recognize certs from eMudhra.

The Indian business then quit the SSL/TLS certification business, which it said was never a major source of revenue but had suddenly become a severe source of embarrassment.

Kumar’s new post lists three steps eMudhra will take to wind up its certification business, one of which will see the company “Put in place improvements motivated by findings of [an] independent review to strengthen our general PKI operations.”

Sounds like a plan. ®

articles.title: Russian cloud Yandex says drone attacks on its datacenters caused data loss
articles.description: Now enables backup by default and hints a little on-prem infra never hurt anyone
articles.content:
Russian cloud operator Yandex has admitted to data loss after a drone attack on one of its datacenters.

The attack, which Ukrainian press said was ordered by Kyiv, happened in early October and caused a fire and subsequent outage at Yandex’s ru-central1-b availability zone. Subsequent strikes targeted more Yandex datacenters and disrupted more of the company’s cloud and payment services.

On Tuesday, Yandex posted an update on its recovery efforts, which it spun as something of a triumph because it restored over 97 percent of customer data. Of course that also means the company lost 2.84 percent of customer data, which it blamed on “critical hardware damage and a lack of backups on the platform.”

It’s unclear if Yandex’s use of the phrase “on the platform” indicates it doesn’t keep backups of its own cloud, if whatever resilience techniques it employs don’t create multiple copies of customer data, or if clients didn’t protect their data.

Whatever happened, Yandex has decided to enable backups by default for all VMs customers create in its cloud.

That decision will mean customers will consume and pay for more Yandex resources, unless they opt out of the automated backups.

Given that drones damaged three Yandex locations, and the war with Ukraine continues, users have good reasons to consider alternatives to its services.

Indeed, Yandex’s announcement of its recovery efforts links to a page extolling the virtues of a hybrid cloud when devising data protection strategies. That page also mentions Yandex’s own Stackland product, which brings its stack on-prem, as an example of a hybrid approach.

On Wednesday the company also launched a new availability zone named ru-central1-f. Yandex didn’t say where it’s located, other than to say it’s in “a new location.” Interestingly, Yandex has imposed quotas that limit the amount of resources users can access in the new availability zone and says it can’t yet handle traffic to private endpoints at the new facility.

Many nations have imposed sanctions that restrict sales of technology products to Russia. It’s therefore unsurprising that Yandex might struggle to provision enough infrastructure to allow untrammeled access to a new availability zone. ®

articles.title: Constantine Director 'Hopeful' for Sequel After DC Studios Shakeup
articles.description: The director of Constantine, Francis Lawrence, opened up about the movie's long-awaited sequel now that DC Studios has had a changing of the guard.
articles.content:
The director of Constantine, Francis Lawrence, opened up about the movie's long-awaited sequel now that DC Studios has had a changing of the guard.

James Gunn and Peter Safran are out at DC Studios in a sudden and unexpected move that has sparked no end of worry and speculation among fans. Gunn, for his part, cited a distaste for the “corporate” side of the job, but confirmed that projects already in motion, like Man of Tomorrow, are still a-go.

Fans aren’t the only ones scratching their heads about what might happen next. Francis Lawrence, the director of oodles of Hollywood blockbusters, is also in this boat — though he’s rather optimistic about the situation, as it means he might finally get the chance to make another Constantine film.

Speaking with Collider ahead of his next movie, The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping, Lawrence clarified that he isn’t happy for anyone to lose their jobs, but admitted that he’s keen on the possibility of getting Constantine 2 off the ground now that things are changing at DC.

"Well, I’ll tell you this,” he began. “Not that I want anybody to lose their jobs, so this is not like a schadenfreude kind of thing, but I will say that we’ve been trying to make Constantine 2 for twenty-something years, and we have an idea, and we have a script, and we’ve been wanting to make it, and the people that were at DC were an impediment to us making it.

“So, we are now more hopeful as of yesterday’s news that maybe now there will be another opportunity. But again, we’ve been trying to make this for twenty-something years, and there’s always been obstacles in the road to making it, and it’s not me, it’s not Keanu, it’s not Akiva. J.J. [Abrams] is on it, as well. We all want to do it. So, it’s really going to be people at Paramount, Warner, whoever’s running DC now, getting everybody on board to say, like, 'Hey, we can do a sequel of our version of Constantine?'"

Lawrence said, without a doubt, that this version of Constantine will be another R-Rated film, no matter what. He explained that the first movie had been made with a PG-13 rating in mind, but despite their best efforts, it was hit with an R label. If given the chance to make a sequel, Lawrence wants to lean all-in and make it a true R-rated experience.

“So, part of the idea from the very beginning was, because we followed all the rules to make a PG-13 movie and we got hit with an R, they told us, 'You can’t do anything about it. It’s going to be an R no matter what.' We tried to fight them on it, and they said, 'Nope. It’s an R,' but really, it’s an R-rated PG-13 movie, which pisses me off,” he explained.

"And so we all kind of came back and said, 'Okay, when we do this next time, we’re making the hard-R version of Constantine.' So when we do it, it’s going to be the hard-R version of Constantine."

Lawrence doubled down on his desire to make another Constantine at all costs, even saying that he doesn’t mind if it gets put into a shared universe or remade to fit DC’s ever-evolving plans at some point. He claimed that he and Keanu would even compromise on their financial compensation to get the film made, if that's what it takes.

"Personally, I don’t even care if somebody has a plan for some sort of shared universe, and they want to do another version of Constantine. If they just let us do the sequel to our version, they can coexist. So, I have renewed hope as of yesterday that there might be some possibility for forward movement there,” he said.

"We have to be responsible,” he continued, speaking about the financial side of the equation. “We want to make it. This is not the kind of movie that I would charge full freight and Keanu could charge full freight. It’s something we have to do, because we love and want to take a gamble on it, and do it responsibly. And so, we’ve been thinking about that same idea for 20 years, that we’re not going to do it for $100 million. We have to be scrappy about it."

Constantine was released in 2005. Starring Keanu Reeves, the movie is based on the DC/Vertigo comic book Hellblazer and follows supernatural detective John Constantine in his mission to purge the world of nefarious evil entities.

This is the latest news about Constantine after Reeves reportedly pitched a sequel to DC Studios in 2025. And just earlier this month, it was revealed that Evil Dead Wrath writer-director Francis Galluppi was hired by DC Studios to write a John Constantine movie for them, though it’s unclear if he’ll also be directing.

articles.title: Monster Hunter Outlanders Review
articles.description: This mobile spin-off maintains the gameplay loop and visuals of its console counterparts, with the caveat of how progress gates push microtransactions.
articles.content:
If there's a singular idea that defines Monster Hunter, it's the grind. Capcom's mega-hit franchise, ever since its inception on the PSP, has flourished because of how it embraces the very idea of grinding and transforms it into an infectiously fun gameplay loop. Repetition and habit are vital parts of the series, so it makes sense, then, that the mobile game gacha format would eventually come to Monster Hunter, fitting currencies and timed gauges into that collecting and grinding experience. But my biggest surprise with Monster Hunter Outlanders has been how it's a comprehensive, full-fledged Monster Hunter packed onto phones and tablets. While it does eventually get buried under an avalanche of currencies to keep track of and some gacha roadblocks, there's enough meat on the bone here to sustain those hungry for more Monster Hunter or a solid action RPG on mobile.

Like most Monster Hunter games, Outlanders follows a group of intrepid explorers from the Adventurer's Guild, this time sent to the uncharted island of Aesolan to investigate a mineral called Radiantate, and how it's influencing various breeds of monsters. After a brief action-packed intro, you're essentially let loose onto the island, free to explore the first environment or tackle the story as you see fit. But also, like most Monster Hunter games, the initial 20 or so hours of Outlanders are extremely guided and layered with seemingly endless tutorials. That's compounded by the nature of being a mobile game, meaning it has to introduce a half-dozen modes, various pull systems, currencies for powering up your Adventurer, and much more.

The most succinct way to describe Outlanders is if you took Monster Hunter World, streamlined its combat, and crammed the entire thing into a mobile game. I almost cannot overstate how closely Outlanders resembles World in every way, even right down to the general structure and story. It takes a bit of an interesting approach, filling the story with a cast of characters that doubles as the big gacha pulls, even though you also have your "main" player-created character. While the overall story feels a bit rote and generic, the world of Outlanders itself is still brimming with things to do. While not a traditional open world game, it's in the exact same framework as Monster Hunter World and Wilds, giving you massive zones to explore. In these zones, you can naturally hunt monsters (without kicking off missions), gather resources, engage in little minigames like a rhythmic one where you steal a flying monster's treasure, and undertake any number of sidequests.

Pocket Hunting

My biggest surprise with Outlanders is how uncompromising the scope of its world feels, right in line with a big mainline Monster Hunter, supported by the fact that this game looks absolutely stunning, and runs like a dream. On an iPhone 14 Plus I was able to run the game on High settings with a stable 45fps, and almost zero slowdown, even during intense battles.

The actual act of exploring the world feels just as entrancing as in major Monster Hunters. Various options for constructing camps and equipment as you explore the world make both traversal and item gathering easier. Camps unlock fast travel points and places to rest, catapults send your adventurer flying on their glider at high speed, and resource collectors constantly soak up those valuable items you need.

Combat is still largely about that push-and-pull of timing, knowing when to pivot between offense and defense, and winding up your attacks at just the right time. That timing and weight of battle has always set Monster Hunter apart from other action games, and it's still present here. But where you can see the mobile limitations is in the particulars of combat control and the various, and many systems, used to improve your Adventurer's stats.

Essentially, Outlanders is a squad-based Monster Hunter, where you build a party consisting of your main character and characters you pull (multiplayer with other actual players is available, too). But you can also play as each of the gacha characters, who have their own movesets, Ultimates, and abilities. For example, Keres uses dual blades that are actually a set of claws, giving her a completely separate set of skills, including one Wolverine-like drill attack. Meanwhile, Luxheart has a two-handed sword that he can rev up to shoot out fireworks, making each of his attacks like a miniature show. These various characters are actually one of my favorite parts of Outlanders, as their designs dig into a bit of tokusatsu pizazz, leaning into the overall goofiness of Monster Hunter as well.

The smart streamlining of combat still keeps the intensity of hunts alive, while being more playable in short bursts. Having distinct movests also goes a long way to breaking up the monotony of repeat hunts and grinding. However, Outlanders overall has fewer weapon types than the last few games as a result, clocking in at eight total weapon types – some notable exclusions being the Hunting Horn and Insect Glaive. And overall, Outlanders plays a bit like a slightly simplified version of World in that it streamlines the more dynamic gameplay. For example, a lot of the emergent world elements, like using a Flashfly to stun a monster, are simple icons that pops up on-screen if you're near.

The bigger change, however, is Outlander's two different control schemes: Adventure and Classic. Adventure boils everything down to three buttons – Attack, React, and Burst – automatically and intuitively altering each of these buttons based on the situation. As examples, the Bowgun will swap ammo based on what's most effective in the moment, or the react button might turn into a guard instead of a dodge.

What we said about Monster Hunter Wilds

"Monster Hunter Wilds continues to smooth off the traditionally rough edges of the series in smart ways, reducing as much friction as possible that could get in the way of you grabbing any of its exceptionally fun weapons and planting them firmly in a monster’s hide. But in that quest to make Monster Hunter more approachable, Wilds has carved a little too close to the bone in some places, trimming its challenge back so much that I barely needed to dig into its in-depth equipment system at all this time to become an apex predator. Its more flexible combat is some of the most fun I’ve had with the series, but like the blustering lighting storms of its gorgeous desert, it'll burns brightly but briefly until Capcom unleashes some real endgame beasts to challenge us." - Tom Marks, February 24, 2025

Score: 8

Read the full review

Classic control mode gives you more fine-tuned control with more dedicated buttons in the vein of a typical Monster Hunter experience. It works fine on a touchscreen, perhaps even a bit better than I was expecting. But if you opt to use touch controls, I'd heavily recommend the Adventure control scheme, simply because Classic is a lot to juggle without a gamepad-style attachment or accessory. I did find the best way to play Outlanders is on Classic with a controller, but of course, that may not be an option for everyone all the time.

Another piece of good news is that Outlanders still shines in terms of monster designs and variety, and that's essential to get right. There's a good array of creatures from across the series, and each monster gets a second souped-up "Radiant" form that adds new attacks and behaviors you need to contend with. Outlanders also still has that wonderful emergent element of World and Wilds where an even bigger predator might stumble into the middle of your battle, forcing you to adapt on the fly.

The simplified control scheme and combat does mean some big changes in how you approach fighting monsters. While you can still climb walls by running up to them, there is no dedicated jump action so you're largely relegated to the ground in fights. Ultimates and skills from your partner characters, like cannons that shoot nets, help add more to the ground game – but sometimes I just wish I could jump on a Rathalos' tail for those thrilling moments I enjoy from the series. By and large, that more streamlined combat experience works for what Outlanders is going for: little snippets and bursts of satisfying gameplay, maybe one quest on the train, or while you're waiting in line somewhere.

Off The Menu

A lot of the core systems of Outlanders click together well, but obviously, the bigger question is how the monetization and gacha systems work. As I said earlier, Monster Hunter has always been about grinding, but finding unique ways to make that grind enjoyable. Unfortunately, Outlanders doesn't always succeed at that second part. When I say the currency and overarching systems of this game can be confusing, I really mean it. I'm no stranger to gacha games, I've seen their evolution over the two decades I've been playing them, but even I had a hard time keeping track of everything I had to juggle in Outlanders.

On top of equipment and partners (like Palicos) for each adventurer, you also have to upgrade their charms, and then ascend said charms once you've reached max level. But in order to boost the max level, you need to raise your Ecological Rank, which also has a number of different requirements. Not to mention that partners have their own leveling system. Then there's the Insight system that adds skills to each adventurer based on skill points they've accrued with weapons. Then there's the Visage system, where you need to "paint" cards of the monsters you take down in the world, as you defeat them. Multiple Visages can be equipped on each character, and every Visage can be ranked up individually.

Oh yeah, and there's Adventurer Rank, Proof of Mastery level, and Investigation Notes – all of which are sort of independent levelling and knowledge systems. Then there are rewards for the specific season the game is on, and different launch initiatives that also have their own currency to gain (and many have optional passes you can purchase for real money to get more rewards). There are a few different gameplay modes on top of all this. You can, of course, follow the main story and simply explore the world. But outside of that, you can take on Free Hunts for specific monsters, use rechargeable Stamina for Hunt Requests to gain levelling items, a lengthy Trial Expedition mode where you take on 150 battles of ascending difficulty, and Guild Clash and Guild Carnival modes where different guilds play together.

Needless to say, there's a metric ton of things to do in Outlanders, and even across 30 hours of playing this game you'll be unlocking new modes, tutorials, and options. If these systems were complementary to that core hunting experience it'd be one thing, but so often Outlanders' deluge of systems simply gets in the way of the action, grinding things down to a halt as you trudge through menus.

To Outlander's credit, I never felt pressured to spend any money in those first 30 hours, and had more materials than I needed. However, at a certain point, the roadblocks do start to pop up, especially as you unlock more gacha characters, and subsequently need to power them up. While you can continue playing Outlanders when those roadblocks hit, it's readily apparent that real money can "optimize" the experience. That becomes doubly true when you see the grind needed for unlocking special costumes or characters in events.

While I think Outlanders is overall one of the more generous gacha games I've played, there are nonetheless points where you will need to grind out activities to continue the story, or even wait a day until you can get more daily rewards. You consistently need to improve your Adventurer Rank, Ecological Level, and more to continue to the next main story quest. Whereas many Monster Hunter games start to open up after

articles.title: Nvidia’s Board reportedly preparing to oust CEO Jensen Huang as second extra-marital affair emerges
articles.description: Nvidia Board reportedly moves to expel Jensen Huang as stock tumbles on latest scandals and lack of succession plans at Nvidia.
articles.content:
Nvidia's Board of Directors is preparing to oust co-founder and chief executive Jensen Huang following revelations of two extramarital affairs, including one with a woman suspected of working for Chinese intelligence and another with an Nvidia executive, reports The Wall Street Journal. Although no final decision has been made yet, the company's directors could meet as early as November 11 to discuss Huang's future. Whoever succeeds Huang will be the company's second CEO in 33 years. Nvidia's stock dropped 8% in after-hours trading following the reports. Nvidia's board of directors launched an independent investigation into the matter on November 8.

The report from the WSJ comes hours after the New York Times revealed that Huang allegedly had an extramarital relationship with Kimberly Powell, Nvidia's vice president of health care, who reports directly to him. According to five people who worked at Nvidia, the relationship was known internally, while Huang and Powell were reportedly seen together at a San Jose hotel during Nvidia's GTC conference in March. The allegations follow an earlier report that Huang had a relationship with Alice Huang, a Chinese businesswoman whom U.S. intelligence believes to be a Chinese intelligence asset.

A similar controversy cost Intel chief executive Brian Krzanich his position in June 2018, when an internal investigation confirmed that he had maintained a consensual relationship with an employee, which violated the company's non-fraternization policy applicable to all managers. It is noteworthy that Nvidia's code of conduct explicitly identifies personal relationships as potential conflicts of interest and instructs employees to consult the company's legal department when such conflicts arise. Whether Huang violated Nvidia's internal policies remains unclear, as the code of conduct does not explicitly prohibit all relationships between managers and subordinates.

Huang's potential departure would mark the first CEO transition in Nvidia's 33-year history, and therefore his succession has become an immediate concern for Nvidia, which does not have anyone of Huang's caliber in the leadership team. Although chief financial officer Colette Kress could potentially serve as interim chief executive if Huang is ousted while the BoD searches for a permanent replacement, it remains to be seen how Wall Street would react to this assignment.

Nvidia co-founder Chris Malachowsky, who used to be the company's senior vice president of engineering and operations and remains a member of the company's board and an Nvidia Fellow, could also play a role in the succession process, given his extensive knowledge of Nvidia's technology, corporate culture, and history. However, has not served in an executive role at Nvidia for at least a decade, so the chances that he will succeed Huang are low.

Back on Sunday, directors expressed confidence in Jensen Huang and his leadership team, a choice of words that did not exactly guarantee his continued tenure.

articles.title: Marvel 1943: Rise of Hydra Is Reportedly 'Close to Done,' Though at the Cost of Cutting Back on Content and Length
articles.description: Marvel 1943: Rise of Hydra, Amy Hennig's Captain America/Black Panther game, is reportedly close to being finished, but it sounds like it may be extremely compromised.
articles.content:
Marvel 1943: Rise of Hydra, Amy Hennig's Captain America/Black Panther game, is reportedly close to being finished, but it could be extremely compromised.

According to a new report from Kotaku, Marvel 1943: Rise of Hydra is "close to done." The news comes hours after rumors began spread online that the game was canceled, with an official announcement coming soon. According to Kotaku and Bloomberg's Jason Schreier, Skydancer leadership told staff via Slack that this is not the case and that they should continue business as usual.

Kotaku's report went on to describe the game's development as difficult, which should come as no surprise to anyone who's been following its journey. The title was announced in 2024 and has been delayed several times, with little to no news or footage beyond that.

Kotaku claims that Marvel 1943: Rise of Hydra initially began as a Netflix game, but was later expanded for consoles and PC. Unfortunately, the title is reportedly "light on gameplay," with most of the action mapped to one button and the experience lacking "significant interactivity."

The project has also allegedly gone well over budget, and as a result, has had to "significantly" scale back from its original vision in terms of content and length. As of right now, we have no idea when Marvel 1943: Rise of Hydra will release, but if it really is nearing the finish line, we could see something next year. Unfortunately, it doesn't seem like the game will be a hyper-engaging action/adventure title with riveting action, from the sound of it.

This is purely speculative, but based on the details from Kotaku's report, it wouldn't be surprising if this is more along the lines of a Quantic Dream experience like Heavy Rain or Detroit: Become Human, with some combat sprinkled in. Either way, if fans were hoping for something like Marvel's Spider-Man, but with Captain America and Black Panther, they may end up pretty disappointed.

Marvel 1943: Rise of Hydra is meant to be director Amy Hennig's first proper game since Uncharted 3 in 2011. Although she has consulted and helped out on some other games like Forspoken over the years, Hennig hasn't led a new game since Uncharted 3. She was reportedly ousted from Naughty Dog in the early 2010s after Uncharted 4 was struggling to meet internal expectations. She then went to EA, where she was meant to lead a new Star Wars game with Visceral Games, but the studio was shut down and the project was scrapped. Now, she's heading up this Marvel game... and we'll just have to wait and see how it turns out.

articles.title: AMC App Experiences Slowdown as Marvel Fans Rush to Buy Doomsday Tickets After VisionQuest Finale
articles.description: So many Marvel fans tried to snag their tickets for Avengers: Doomsday after watching the VisionQuest season finale that they literally crashed the AMC Theaters app.
articles.content:
So many Marvel fans tried to snag their tickets for Avengers: Doomsday after watching the VisionQuest season finale that they literally crashed the AMC Theatres app. At least, that's what users are saying.

The crash reportedly occurred on the night of November 10 — the same night that the VisionQuest finale aired, which included a post-credits scene that all but confirmed a particular character will show up in Avengers: Doomsday.

Shortly after the episode aired on Disney+, fans and Marvel fanpages shared that the AMC app was showing an error message when they tried to use it, which asked them to “please try again.” They were unable to navigate to other pages within the app; it seems that it was totally unusable during this time.

Of course, viewers instantly pointed to the VisionQuest season finale as the reason for this, indicating that the hype levels were high enough to warrant a mass of fan interest in seeing Doomsday in theaters.

In a statement to IGN, an AMC Theatres spokesperson revealed that there was a 30-minute period where "some transactions were taking longer than normal." The spokesperson said that the AMC app didn't outright crash, as data showed that tickets continued to get sold throughout this period, but indicated that some users may have run into that error message during that time.

Warning: Major spoilers for VisionQuest below!

It’s no surprise that Marvel fans got so excited about Doomsday after this. The finale’s post-credits scene, which was also kept a secret from the media, showed Wanda Maximoff, aka the Scarlet Witch, having an interaction with Doctor Doom.

The specific scene returns to the ending of Doctor Strange in the Multiverse of Madness, in which the Scarlet Witch sacrifices herself by destroying the Darkhold. While viewers were under the impression that her heroic decision ultimately lead to her death, this isn’t the case. Doctor Doom appears and frees her from the rubble that had collapsed on top of her, saying, "Scarlet Witch, awaken. Your power will be mine." She comes to with a shocked expression before the scene ends.

Given that the Scarlet Witch has been officially confirmed to be alive after four years of ambiguity, fans are understandably beside themselves with excitement. On social media, viewers wasted no time sharing their hype for the scene in response to AMC’s app crash, with one writing, “That’s the Scarlet Witch effect!”

“Wanda impact,” another wrote, while another said the crash happened “all because of Wanda Maximoff!”

“Mother is that powerful,” another superfan said. “We’re ready to support anything she does because she can do no wrong.”

Avengers: Doomsday releases in theaters on December 18, 2026. While you’re waiting, you can watch Avengers: Endgame Encore, which has been re-released with new scenes and will be available to stream on Disney+ this Friday.

articles.title: Nvidia Board Is Preparing to Potentially Oust CEO Jensen Huang
articles.description: Three days after launching an independent investigation into CEO Jensen Huang, the Nvidia board is reportedly preparing to oust the executive.
articles.content:
Three days after launching an independent investigation into CEO Jensen Huang, the Nvidia board is reportedly preparing to oust the executive.

Nvidia's board will be meeting as soon as today to discuss Huang's future after an extramarital affair with Alice Huang, a suspected Chinese spy, according to The Wall Street Journal. That affair was first reported by The New York Times and was followed up by a statement issued by Nvidia on Sunday, saying it'd be investigating its CEO. According to a new report from The New York Times, he'd also engaged in a second affair with an executive who reported to him.

This meeting follows an investigation that was announced on Sunday. In that announcement, Nvidia said, "The Board prioritizes U.S. national and economic security, which is paramount to the interests of Nvidia and its shareholders. While the Board has no reason to believe that either national security or Nvidia secrets were compromised, the Board's inquiry will examine all available information. Jensen fully supports the review and has committed to cooperating with it."

Huang then issued a letter to employees, obtained by the BBC, where he admitted that he was unfaithful and apologized for hurting his wife and children.

In many ways, Jensen Huang is the face of AI in the U.S., and so it makes sense that Nvidia's board would want to get this situation under control. The company's chips power nearly every AI model that's currently running, and so a security breach of this scale is a massive liability. Huang is a co-founder of Nvidia and has been running the company since 1993, so his ousting could have huge ramifications.

IGN has reached out to Nvidia for comment and will update this story as soon as communications have been received.

articles.title: Henry Cavill Is Open to Returning as Superman Once Again
articles.description: Henry Cavill has stated that he's still open to the idea of playing Superman following all the shake-ups at DC Studios.
articles.content:
Henry Cavill has stated that he's still open to the idea of playing Superman following all the shake-ups at DC Studios.

In an interview with Inverse, Cavill was asked if he'd ever be interested in playing Superman again, and the interviewer suggested the Kingdom Come storyline as a possibility. Cavill noted he would never say never to the idea, and that there are a lot of "fantastic storylines" to adapt for Superman.

"Look, there's lots of fantastic storylines. There's always a lot of opportunity. As the pigeon sang to Fievel in An American Tail, 'never say never.' And I buy into that. I’ve had such a wonderful time playing Superman in the past. I would never say never now."

Of course, the timing of these comments could not come at a more interesting moment. If this happened a week ago, no one would've thought much of it. However, earlier this week, DC Studios heads James Gunn and Peter Safran were ousted from the company. They remain on board until December 1, when a new head, Jeremy Latcham, will take over. Latcham is expected to make changes to DC's direction, possibly resulting in a reboot, though that has yet to be firmly decided. His ultimate vision, however, is to focus on DC's mainstream characters in an effort to quickly assemble the Justice League on the big screen.

Presumably, they'll wait until James Gunn's Superman sequel, Man of Tomorrow, hits theaters in July to make a decision on whether they'll reboot or recast this DC universe. Cavill has famously been through a lot as Superman. His debut film, Man of Steel, was controversial thanks to the absurd casualties in his fight with General Zod. Batman v Superman also caused some friction with fans for a variety of reasons, one of which was that Superman was extremely brooding and miserable.

After the catastrophic disaster that was Justice League, Cavill's role as Superman remained in question. There were rumors he would be replaced, while others indicated the powers that be simply weren't sure what to do with him. Eventually, Dwayne 'The Rock' Johnson went above all of the WB execs and brought the actor back for a cameo in 2022's Black Adam, five years after Cavill's last appearance in the role. He was promised new Superman adventures... but then, James Gunn took over DC just weeks later, and Cavill was essentially let go from the role.

The fact that Cavill is open to taking another crack at things after all of that is certainly interesting. Whether that opportunity ever comes remains to be seen, but it seems hard to imagine the new leadership reviving the Snyderverse.
