articles.title: AWS had its agents build a free and open emulator for AWS. They now maintain it, too.
articles.description: AWS on Wednesday launched an emulator for AWS called AWS Emulator. That, by itself, is interesting and may raise some The post AWS had its agents build a free and open emulator for AWS. They now maintain it, too. appeared first on The New Stack .
articles.content:
AWS on Wednesday launched an emulator for AWS called AWS Emulator.

That, by itself, is interesting and may raise some questions about the future of LocalStack. But what’s maybe most interesting is that the emulator was entirely built by a team of agents and will also be maintained by them going forward.

Since AWS wasn’t sure it could actually copyright the work of these agents — and didn’t want to assert copyright where none may exist — the emulator is available under the Creative Commons Zero license, which puts the code into the public domain.

Tom ‘Spot’ Callaway, a principal open source software strategist at AWS, told The New Stack that there have obviously been other emulators in the past — and AWS itself has built some, too.

“The challenge is that they get out of date very quickly,” he explains. “They don’t always reflect reality on the ground, and because of that, they’re often not trusted. And we didn’t even trust them internally.”

With the rise of agentic coding tools, the team also saw a need for a better emulator that could help agents test code against AWS services without having to hand over AWS credentials to the agents.

The agent system building AWS Emulator. Credit: AWS.

Meanwhile, the team was also looking at a test case for building a full project with agents, and the emulator proved to be a good testing ground, in large part because it provided a bounded problem with clear goals and the ability to test the results.

Since AWS already publishes a full set of API models as Smithy models and generates all its SDKs from those files, “there’s no reason that we can’t also generate mock emulation around that same logic,” Callaway says.

A weekend Kiro experiment

The project goes back to an experiment by Matt Goldberg, a senior principal engineer on the AWS Developer Tools team. Callaway says the team was “heavily inspired by the Anthropic work where they instantiated a compiler,” referring to the C compiler that Anthropic researchers had a team of agents build earlier this year.

Goldberg writes in a blog post that he first asked Kiro, AWS’s agentic coding tool, to build an emulator for Amazon Simple Queue Service (SQS). It came back with a first version 15 minutes later. He then had Kiro build out the rest of AWS over a weekend. That version unsurprisingly had gaps, he notes, but his team started testing its own software against it the following Monday.

“I got to admit, the first time I heard about this, I was like, ‘Are we sure this is a good idea?’” Callaway says.

The more the team iterated on it, he adds, the more comfortable he became that this was a good problem for agents to take on.

In its current version, AWS Emulator supports 438 public AWS API models covering more than 200 services. As AWS updates them and releases new services, the agents will quickly update the emulator, too.

Callaway expects the gap between a new AWS service launching and the emulator supporting it to be “days, not weeks, not months,” though he notes the team hasn’t yet seen how that plays out with the project in public.

The emulator itself is written in Rust and runs locally on Linux, macOS, and Windows, without a network connection or an AWS account.

“There’s no AI inside of AWS Emulator,” Callaway says. “It does not do an LLM callout at all.”

Three teams of agents

AWS says it divides the work among three teams of agents. The first develops test scenarios from the public Smithy models and runs them against real AWS services to establish how the emulator should behave.

These scenarios can involve several services working together, rather than just individual API calls. As Callaway explains, “if the docs don’t tell the truth, then the cloud becomes the source of truth.”

The second team runs those scenarios against the emulator and investigates where its behavior differs from AWS. It groups failures that appear to have a common cause and files issues in the code repository.

Finally, the third team picks up those issues and changes the code to address them. Before those changes can merge, they have to pass build and test checks, as well as reviews by other agents for security problems, coding standards, and regressions in the emulator’s behavior.

The human engineers, meanwhile, focus on improving the system that directs the agents.

“We don’t edit it. We don’t modify it,” Callaway says of the emulator’s code. “If we find that the code has issues, we try and trace those issues back to the agent and fix the agent so that it doesn’t make bad code.”

So when there is a problem in the code those agents generated, the team will change how the agents work, rather than patch the code by hand.

Goldberg writes that an earlier version of the agents at one point decided to write their own Python interpreter so the emulator could support Lambda functions. The team has since instructed them to reuse existing libraries.

“I think we’ve learned a lot about sandboxing,” Callaway says, “haven’t we all in the last few months?”

The first iterations of the system “did not have as aggressive a sandbox as they needed to,” he says, and there was some early concern about the agents looking at the source code of AWS’s internal services to figure out how to implement something like Aurora. The team also spent a lot of time reassuring Amazon executives that the framework building the emulator wasn’t going to “go rogue.”

No pull requests accepted

That hands-off approach goes for outside contributors, too.

“We’re not going to take pull requests on the project at all,” Callaway says. “The agents will be doing that. We will take issues from customers.”

He describes the agents as “their own little pull request army.” If they keep getting a particular API wrong, “that’s a bug in the agent,” he says, and he expects customers to mostly contribute scenarios the emulator doesn’t handle well yet.

AWS is also publishing the benchmark it uses to test the emulator “so that you can not trust us,” Callaway says. “You can run that benchmark.” Others could also use it to benchmark their own work, he notes.

What the emulator can’t do

Users shouldn’t expect the emulator to do the things the actual services do, though.

“I run this SQL query, and I don’t get the right results,” Callaway says. “Well, guess what? There’s no database.” The emulator, he says, “really was built for the purposes of testing coverage.”

AWS says it will share more about the project at its re:Invent conference, which starts Nov. 30. The New Stack will be there — and we’re even throwing a party.

articles.title: Developers have been hacking around MCP’s file-upload problem for two years. A fix is taking shape.
articles.description: The Model Context Protocol (MCP) has played an instrumental part in connecting AI assistants to external tools and data since The post Developers have been hacking around MCP’s file-upload problem for two years. A fix is taking shape. appeared first on The New Stack .
articles.content:
The Model Context Protocol (MCP) has played an instrumental part in connecting AI assistants to external tools and data since Anthropic launched the project some two years ago. Want to have a coding agent check the status of a bug? Give it access to your issue tracker through an MCP server. Or ask an assistant how many orders your company shipped last week? Connect it to a tool that can query your database.

Part of the Agentic AI Foundation since last December, MCP has a roadmap that reflects the demands of running the protocol in production. For instance, maintainers have been working to make servers easier to deploy without keeping track of individual client sessions, and to let companies manage access through their existing identity systems.

But a perennial problem developers have faced is how to pass a file from an AI app to an MCP tool. For example, say you attach a PDF to a chat and ask the assistant to save it to cloud storage — the assistant can call a tool to save the file, but developers still have to work out how to get the PDF from the chat app to the tool. That can mean issuing a temporary upload link, or perhaps sending the user to a separate upload page.

To address this gap, the folks at the MCP project have outlined a draft extension that gives clients and tools a common way to handle uploads and downloads.

MCP’s finally tackling the file-upload problem

Why MCP needs a way to move files

In a blog post published on Tuesday, Den Del i marsky, lead maintainer of MCP and member of technical staff at Anthropic, and Google software engineer Wil St. Charles, lay out the rationale for the new extension, noting that developers’ needs have changed as they’ve started asking agents to do more with the tools MCP connects them to.

“Many of those MCP server projects now need to work with files — often driven by increasing agent capabilities and autonomy.”

“Over the past two years, the things people build with the protocol have become more ambitious. Much more ambitious,” they write. “Many of those MCP server projects now need to work with files — often driven by increasing agent capabilities and autonomy.”

This demand has shown up in the community more or less since MCP’s inception. In December 2024, a developer building a tool to process files asked on GitHub how to get a file from the client to the server. An Anthropic team member acknowledged the difficulty and said they were exploring how a tool could send a file back to an AI app. Other community members subsequently chipped in with advice, with one noting that they had built their own way to send files from the AI app to the MCP server. Their MCP client uploaded the file directly to the server before calling the tool, with the upload itself happening outside the protocol.

Developers have been looking for ways to hack around the gap ever since. In one Reddit thread a few months back, one user said a temporary S3 upload link worked in Claude once outbound access was enabled, but they couldn’t get the same approach working in ChatGPT, so they built a separate web app and upload page. Another developer said they had built a drag-and-drop interface to an MCP App, which let users submit files themselves but still left the agent without a way to initiate the upload on its own.

There are packaged options, too. FastMCP offers a drag-and-drop upload component for developers building MCP Apps, while Box recently launched secure file upload and download support for PDFs and Office documents through its own MCP server.

The folks at the MCP project, for their part, have been slowly working toward a common standard. Delimarsky opened an exploratory upload proposal in August 2025, and a File Uploads Working Group, initially made up of members from Anthropic and OpenAI, followed in April. In October, the group added file downloads to its remit.

Now, a draft specification sets out how transfers in both directions could work.

“While we have the shape outlined, we’re not sure yet that what we started with is what we’ll end up with.”

“While we have the shape outlined, we’re not sure yet that what we started with is what we’ll end up with,” the authors write. “The best way to find out is, you guessed it — contact with reality.”

How MCP would move files

The experimental file-transfer extension builds on the framework for extensions MCP introduced in July to let clients and servers opt into new features without changing the core protocol. The experimental stage gives developers a place to prototype and refine an idea before, or alongside, a formal Specification Enhancement Proposal (SEP).

Either way, the file itself bypasses the model.

Under the extension, if you ask an assistant to save an attached PDF to cloud storage, for example, the model calls the tool and the MCP client handles the upload. The client can send a small file within the tool request, and for a larger file, the client uploads it separately and calls the tool again to finish the job. Either way, the file itself bypasses the model.

For downloads, a tool that exports a CSV, for example, can include a download URL once it’s finished producing the file. The client can then fetch the CSV directly, and the model gets a message telling it what the tool produced.

One of the big security implications centres around how much control the host should have over where files go. As things stand, the proposed extension limits when a client can send its MCP credentials to an upload destination. The host asks the user to approve the upload before the MCP server supplies that destination, so the user may not know where the file will go when they approve it.

“These safeguards control where the client’s MCP credential is sent, but they don’t by themselves control where the file goes,” the authors write.

So a user who thinks they’re saving a confidential PDF to company storage could end up sending it to an endpoint controlled by a malicious server operator. The authors recommend limiting external uploads to approved destinations, and are asking whether hosts should be required to enforce that restriction.

It’s worth noting that developers can prototype against the draft today by implementing the proposed transfer on a test client and server. However, there’s no formal reference implementation yet.

“That’s because we expect that a lot of the inner workings will, in fact, be quite different once we start integrating our experiment with third-party file services, such as cloud storage, database import/export, and many others that require file input and output,” the authors add.

The MCP maintainers say they are targeting a stable release by year-end, and support will remain optional — developers who choose to skip the extension won’t need to change their existing MCP clients or servers.

articles.title: Scientists check their work and confirm it with update on iconic black hole image
articles.description: And find they were right all along
articles.content:
The image of the red ring around the black hole M87, produced by the Event Horizon Telescope (EHT) array, made front-page news around the world in 2019. There was one problem: there was a slim chance the depiction might be wrong.

This week, a small team of four Australian researchers have published their work confirming the result based on a new machine learning algorithm using the same base data.

The 2019 Event Horizon Telescope (EHT) image came from hundreds of scientists working together to capture the first direct view of a black hole's shadow. The measurements were taken at eight telescopes around the world, at locations including Chile, the US, and Antarctica.

Reconstructing the image from the data so geographically distant meant instrument and environment errors could influence the accuracy of the resulting image. Potentially, alternative analyses of the data could have reconstructed an image without the iconic ring shape.

Samuel Lai – a postdoctoral fellow at the Commonwealth Scientific and Industrial Research Organisation (CSIRO) in Western Australia – and his team created an independent imaging algorithm to process the historic dataset to validate the result. The new approach used closed triplets (using three telescopes for error correction) rather than station pairs in an effort to reduce error.

To the relief of the EHT team, the new image recreated the iconic ring-like image seen in the original, according to a paper published in Nature today.

In a prepared statement, Lai said taking pictures of black holes was not easy. "It is like standing in your backyard and trying to take a photo of a doughnut on the Moon," he said.

He explained that when his team applied new advanced machine learning and artificial intelligence techniques to the original Event Horizon Telescope dataset, they found a black hole almost identical in size and shape to the historic EHT image.

"Importantly, our model had no idea what a black hole looked like when we applied it to the M87 data. This is the first truly independent validation of the EHT image, an important step in the scientific process," he said.

Event Horizon Telescope director Laurent Loinard welcomed the new study. "It is extremely gratifying to see that an elegant, entirely independent method recovers the ring structure of M87 across several years, in excellent agreement with the EHT Collaboration's published results," he said. ®

articles.description: It’s that time of year again: Thousands of delegates, lobbyists, and journalists are gathered for the annual UN climate talks, taking place this time in Antalya, Turkey. It’s that time of year again: Thousands of delegates, lobbyists, and journalists are gathered for the annual UN climate talks, taking place this time in Antalya, Turkey.

COP31 officially kicked off on November 8, marking the beginning of negotiations on one of the biggest stages of the climate world. Turkey and Australia are cohosting this year’s talks, which are scheduled to wrap up on November 20.

This annual gathering can often serve as an indicator of where the world stands on addressing and adapting to the climate crisis. And this year’s talks are sure to be a doozy—expect a lot of back and forth on fossil fuels and climate finance in particular. Here’s what you should know about COP31.

In recent years, the tension always feels high when COP rolls around. (COP stands for “Conference of the Parties.”) But this year feels especially charged: The world is still grappling with the ongoing war in Iran, which has disrupted the Middle East and sent economic shock waves around the world as energy prices have spiked.

This year’s COP will be the second without a formal delegation from the US. President Trump formally withdrew the country from the Paris Agreement earlier this year and is in the process of withdrawing from the UN Framework Committee on Climate Change. That’s the treaty that allows formal participation in negotiations.

Meanwhile, things aren’t looking good for the Paris Agreement, which was established at UN climate talks 11 years ago, setting a goal of limiting warming to 1.5 °C over preindustrial levels. In a report published in September, the UN Environment Program acknowledged that global warming is set to exceed that 1.5 °C goal, “likely within the next few years.”

So as climate talks kick off, there’s an obvious, urgent question looming about how to quickly cut emissions to limit warming. There’s also the major issue of how to pay for efforts to address emissions and to help a warming world endure the inevitable damage.

Two years ago, talks ended in a goal of mobilizing $300 billion per year by 2035 to help pay to reduce emissions and adapt to climate change. (Rich nations provided $136.7 billion in 2024, according to the Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development. ) And last year, the COP30 agreement included a goal of tripling the money for adaptation over that period. (Such funding has been quite flat over the past few years.)

The world got a tragic reminder of just how high the stakes are earlier this year, when a glacier collapse caused devastating flooding in the Himalayas. The flood killed approximately 1,500 people, left over 5,000 missing, and caused nearly $5 billion in damage. The UN loss and damages fund committed $20 million to helping Nepal recover (less than 1% of the total estimated cost to the country).

Another key trend to watch is how the formal negotiations engage with the topic of fossil fuels. Three years ago, the final agreement text explicitly called for a transition away from them. But it felt as if things took a step back last year, when the final agreement didn’t even mention the phrase “fossil fuels” once. This will be an interesting conversation, especially because cohosts Turkey and Australia have both faced criticism over their relationships with these fuels—Australia is a major exporter of coal and natural gas, and Turkey’s grid relies heavily on fossil fuels, including coal.

Outside the formal negotiations, COP31 president Murat Kurum, Turkey’s environment minister, is spearheading a side agenda, including two informal initiatives that will be worth watching. These wouldn’t be part of the official agreement text, but countries could sign on to signal support.

One is a pledge to make AI more sustainable; this is almost comically squishy, even as voluntary COP pledges go. The text includes explicit wording that it creates no new obligations for countries, so don’t expect anything resembling enforcement there.

The COP leadership is also pushing to make electricity a larger part of member countries’ energy use. Today, only about 23% of global energy is used in the form of electricity. Fossil fuels, like gasoline in vehicles or natural gas for heating, make up the bulk of the rest. Shifting to more electricity use, and relying on cleaner sources for that electricity, could help drive down emissions. The new pledge’s target is for electricity to make up 35% of total energy consumption by 2035.

With leadership billing this as an “implementation COP,” it would be great to see some real, tangible progress on the global challenge of addressing climate change. I’m not expecting anything groundbreaking, but we’ll be tuned in to see what the final agreement shapes up to be.

articles.title: OpenAI and Georgia county leaders hit with Mafia-style RICO racketeering lawsuit over $30 billion AI data center
articles.description: The plaintiffs alleged that the parties committed fraud and concealment through NDAs and misleading public statements.
articles.content:
Residents of Effingham County, Georgia, just filed a RICO lawsuit against their county commissioners, county leaders, and OpenAI and its affiliates, alleging that they committed various offenses in a conspiracy to get OpenAI’s “Project Camellia” approved. According to the Effingham Herald, the plaintiffs — Dr. Michelle Finch-Mincey, Lehman Mincey Jr., and Raymond Carver — are seeking civil damages, saying that the project has harmed their property values and even pointing out that purchase offers for nearby residential properties have dropped or been withdrawn since the data center was announced.

Go deeper with TH Premium: AI and data centers

(Image credit: Microsoft) The data center cooling state of play

Demand for data center CPUs has surged, and AI agents are responsible

The lawsuit names all Effingham County Commissioners — Chairperson Damon Rahn, Forrest Floyd, Roger Burdette, Jamie DeLoach, Elizabeth Helmly, and Phil Kieffer — as defendants, alongside County Manager Tim Callanan, Effingham County Industrial Development Authority (IDA) CEO Brandt Herndon, the IDA itself, OpenAI, Octans GA LLC, the entity operating the data center on behalf of OpenAI, and Savannah Industrial Development LLC, the agency involved in the sale of IDA property to Octans and OpenAI.

It’s alleged that the defendants committed fraud and concealment through non-disclosure agreements and misleading public statements so that residents remain unaware of the nature of the projects for as long as possible, and that there was a civil conspiracy “to advance Project Camellia through confidential negotiations and closed-door decisions.” They also claimed that the parties engaged in improper land transactions, zoning violations, and civil racketeering.w

Project Camellia is one of OpenAI’s biggest data center projects planned for construction in Effingham County. The site is expected to cost somewhere between $20 billion and $30 billion, to be built across five phases, with a planned compute capacity of 3.2 gigawatts. The company also promised that it will not affect the community’s utility costs, as it will pay for the full cost of all its required infrastructure upgrades, and that it will have minimal water use due to its closed-loop water system. Despite those promises, it seems that some people are opposing the project because of how the county had allegedly tried to secure the land, tax incentives, and zoning approvals without informing the residents until key decisions were finalized and contracts had been signed.

The RICO Act — or Racketeer Influenced and Corrupt Organizations Act — was originally conceived as a way to counter organized crime, particularly Mafia leadership, who often used low-level members to commit individual crimes and do the dirty work for them. However, Georgia’s RICO Act is less stringent than the federal version, which is why it’s been used multiple times for cases that seemingly had nothing to do with the Mafia. For example, it was in the 2023 election racketeering case against Donald Trump and 18 others in the attempt to overturn the 2020 U.S. presidential election results in the state, and it was also used in Young Thug’s trial after the rapper was accused of running YSL Records as a criminal street gang.

Critics say that Georgia’s version is way too encompassing, though, and that it was being used to squeeze defendants involved in more mundane or common felonies. “When you have a hammer, everything looks like a nail,” Georgia State University professor of criminal justice and criminology Volkan Topalli said in Atlanta Magazine.

The actions of both state officials, OpenAI, and its affiliates are not new, though. There have already been multiple complaints of data center developers and local governments using non-disclosure agreements (NDAs) while they negotiate terms for possible data center projects. Developers say they use this tool to avoid “running afoul of insider trading rules,” but people have pointed out that West Feliciana Parish in Louisiana was able to close a data center deal without resorting to one. An AWS data center in Gilroy, California, is also facing scrutiny after residents only discovered the nature of the project when construction began after a five-year permitting saga that relied on zoning rules that were set 45 years ago.

articles.description: We’re a team of five engineers, and we used to wake the on-call engineer three or four times a week The post Why Nitric stopped asking one AI agent to do everything appeared first on The New Stack .
articles.content:
We’re a team of five engineers, and we used to wake the on-call engineer three or four times a week over production incidents. Most were noise rather than serious outages, but at two in the morning, being overly cautious seemed preferable to letting a genuine problem slip through the cracks.

We’ve since reduced both unnecessary overnight interruptions and recurring issues by iterating on triage and following investigations through to fixes. Specialized AI agents help us investigate incidents, organize follow-up work, and prepare changes, with engineers reviewing and correcting the work along the way.

What surprised us was how much more comfortable we became relying on the process. Engineers could inspect an assessment, challenge its assumptions, and use those corrections to improve how we handled later incidents. As follow-up fixes addressed recurring issues, we felt more confident about when to wake the on-call engineer.

That experience has made us question the shape of the work we give our agents. A capable coding agent could potentially investigate an incident, raise a ticket, and prepare a fix, so why divide those responsibilities?

“When an agent’s work needs correction, can you identify the responsibility involved and make a change you can evaluate independently?”

For us, it’s about improving one part of the workflow and judging whether the change helped. When an agent’s work needs correction, can you identify the responsibility involved and make a change you can evaluate independently?

A shared workspace for people and agents

We’re building Sugabots as an open-source, self-hosted workspace where a team can work with several agents on the same task. Engineers can ask questions, contribute evidence, review findings, and bring in another agent, with those exchanges available to other participants.

We organize that work into shared environments called pods, with connections to external systems through MCP. Each agent can have its own model and instructions, while the pod’s connections and tool policies define the access its agents share. The team can configure agents for specific responsibilities and refine their instructions as engineers review the work. Our incident workflow has helped us explore which responsibilities benefit from that separation.

How we run incident triage in Sugabots

Our incident workflow depends on each engineer or agent being able to continue from the evidence, decisions, and corrections recorded during the investigation.

Our Sentry triage agent investigates new, regressed, or escalating issues and decides whether to alert the on-call engineer, request an in-hours review, hand a small fix directly to an implementation agent, or keep the issue in Sentry for monitoring. It records follow-up work in Linear, where a backlog agent helps organize tickets, and the implementation agent can prepare a GitHub pull request for review.

Our incident workflow: agents handle distinct responsibilities while engineers contribute to the shared investigation. Engineers can take on any of the contributions shown.

Engineers participate throughout, reviewing findings, challenging urgency assessments, correcting assumptions, and deciding whether to ship a proposed change. The investigation remains available as work moves between people and agents.

Safeguards back that growing confidence. The instructions call for urgent escalation when an issue could plausibly be a production outage, and urgency is uncertain. Issues classified as noise are archived until escalating, and Sentry retains a direct spike-alert route to incident.io as a backup.

The follow-up matters as much as the initial assessment. Previously, the on-call engineer might investigate an alert, determine it could wait until office hours, and return to other work. Recording the underlying problem in the backlog and prioritizing it gave the team a chance to resolve it before the next on-call engineer encountered the same alert.

Having the backlog agent record follow-up work in Linear gives the team a consistent way to prioritize fixes for the recurring issues behind the interruptions.

Specialize around a decision

We configure each agent for a particular responsibility, choosing its model and instructions to suit the work and defining what a useful result looks like.

We chose Opus 5.5 for Sentry triage, and its instructions cover evidence gathering, classification, escalation, handoffs, and recovery from tool failures. This abbreviated excerpt shows the decisions we ask it to make:

Inspect the full Sentry issue, including customer impact, affected users, release, and event trend, then check for existing tickets or incidents.

Choose an outcome:

Urgent: active customer harm requiring immediate attention; alert the on-call engineer through incident.io.

In-hours review: a defect requiring engineering judgment that can wait; notify the on-call engineer at low urgency.

Auto-fix: a small, non-urgent code change outside restricted areas such as authentication, billing, and migrations; brief the implementation agent to prepare a PR.

No action: expected or transient noise; archive until escalating so a spike brings it back.

State the evidence and uncertainty behind the decision. Implementation briefs must stand alone and include the relevant findings and links.

The backlog manager’s instructions reflect the decisions involved in organizing follow-up work: checking for duplicates, looking up the current Linear cycle, and distinguishing actionable work from issues that need an engineer to clarify scope or make a design decision. Those rules provide defaults while preserving the team’s explicit choices about priority, assignment, and scheduling, and we can refine them independently of the criteria used to assess an incident’s urgency.

Triage and implementation make a useful comparison. Triage asks whether the available evidence justifies interrupting an engineer. Implementation asks what change would resolve the problem and how to verify it. Those decisions have different failure modes: a missed urgent incident, an unnecessary interruption, or a plausible fix that introduces another bug.

“Triage asks whether the available evidence justifies interrupting an engineer. Implementation asks what change would resolve the problem and how to verify it. Those decisions have different failure modes.”

We’ve found it useful to maintain those responsibilities separately because we can refine how incidents are classified while keeping the implementation instructions stable. If an investigation leads to an ineffective fix, we can examine the assessment’s accuracy, the evidence preserved in the ticket, and how the implementation addressed the recorded problem. Each gives us a specific part of the workflow to improve.

Each responsibility also gives us concrete questions to evaluate:

Triage: Did it escalate genuinely urgent incidents? Did it unnecessarily interrupt an engineer?

Backlog management: Did it record the follow-up work, recognize existing tickets, and preserve enough evidence to act on it?

Implementation: Did the proposed change address the problem, and what did an engineer need to correct before accepting it?

We need to evaluate the reduction in wake-up calls alongside how we handle genuinely urgent incidents, including any that triage missed. Fewer interruptions could reflect both better classification and fixes that reduce the volume of incidents arriving. Those outcomes help us judge how the workflow is performing and where to improve it.

The same question applies to the agents already in your workflow: when their output improves, can you explain what improved and what evidence supports that judgment? Separating responsibilities gives you a narrower decision to examine and a clearer basis for evaluating changes.

Match permissions to responsibilities

Separating responsibilities also helps us decide which tool actions each agent needs and when an engineer should approve them.

Our triage instructions include specific write actions: creating Linear issues, sending alerts through incident.io, and archiving Sentry issues until escalating. Tool access needs to reflect those responsibilities, including which actions require an engineer’s approval.

Agent-specific instructions define responsibilities within the access available to the pod; they do not enforce separate permissions for agents sharing that pod.

In Sugabots, the team configures tool-level Off, Ask, and Allow policies on a pod’s connections, and every agent in that pod inherits those policies. Configuring them once gives the team a consistent set of rules for automatic actions, engineer approvals, and disabled tools, including when another agent joins the work.

Triage needs access to evidence and a way to escalate, while implementation needs enough access to prepare a change. Genuinely different access boundaries require separate enforcement, potentially through different pods with different tool policies or appropriately scoped connections. Merge and deployment authority also need explicit policies and, where available, appropriately scoped credentials.

Separate the working context from the investigation

There are three things here with different useful lifetimes:

Configuration: the maintained model, instructions, tools, and expectations for a responsibility.

Execution context: the messages and tool results available to the model while it works on a particular task.

Shared history: the record of evidence, hypotheses, corrections, and decisions that people and agents accumulate.

Consider an investigation where the agent rules out an outage and concludes that an issue can wait until office hours. After enough tool calls, its context may need to be compacted. A summary might preserve the conclusion while omitting the evidence that ruled out the outage.

That detail becomes important if an engineer challenges the assessment. Keeping the original history gives them a way to inspect the reasoning and evidence behind the summary. The agent can work with a compacted context while the fuller record remains available for inspection or retrieval.

To continue the investigation, the next agent needs the relevant evidence and corrections selected from that record and passed along in a brief, or retrieved as it works. Preserving the conversation gives us a source to draw from; selecting the working context remains an explicit part of the handover.

Keep people in the investigation

The same distinction matters when work moves between engineers. An engineer may recognize a pattern the agent missed or explain why an apparently sensible fix would introduce a regression elsewhere in the codebase. That contribution needs to remain available to the engineer or agent continuing the investigation or preparing the fix.

In separate chats, people become responsible for carrying those corrections across. Even when both agents can inspect the same repository and tickets, each conversation contains a different account of what the team has learned.

The reviewer and author relay findings and corrections between their separate chats.

In Sugabots, engineers can contribute to the shared discussion, leaving their corrections alongside the findings that prompted them. The next engineer can see how the investigation changed direction, and an agent continuing the work can receive that correction with its brief.

Engineers and agents contribute to a shared discussion that preserves their findings and corrections.

MCP gives the agent access to evidence, while a shared workspace gives the team access to the investigation.

A staged Sentry triage conversation rendered in the actual Sugabots interface. The messages, event counts, issue reference, and handoff are scripted demonstration data, showing how an engineer’s correction can remain alongside the assessment and implementation brief.

articles.title: PC peripheral maker Logitech giving all of its 7,000 employees the day off to play GTA 6
articles.description: Accessory maker Logitech has a new "Logi Game Day" initiative that allows employees to take a day off from now until this time next year to play a game of their choice — including the one everyone is talking about.
articles.content:
As GTA 6, the most anticipated game of the year, perhaps the decade, nears its November 19 release date, one company has offered its employees the chance to take the day off to play it. Amid the expectation that gamers around the globe will call in sick to play the game instead of heading into the office, PC peripheral and hardware outfit Logitech is getting ahead of the game by giving 7,000 employees the chance to take a day off to play it. Or, if they prefer, they can play any other game instead, the company confirmed in a press release detailing the move.

The new initiative is called "Logi Game Day," and it isn't only available to the top brass. Interns and full-time employees alike can take a day off from now until this time next year, at a time when it's been estimated that the GTA 6 launch could see the U.S. economy take a $1 billion hit in terms of productivity. The game, which is a console exclusive ahead of a claimed early 2027 PC release, is already available for preorder, with pre-loading also up and running. It's a good job, too, with a 212GB PS5 download set to be a real downer for eager gamers with slow internet. The ongoing price hikes also mean that upgrading your PS5 storage for GTA 6 won't be a fun time, either.

As for Logitech, the company believes that it's time for people to move away from the belief that playing games is a waste of time, hence its new initiative. It makes sense for a company that makes gaming accessories to say that, of course, but CEO Hanneke Faber argues that the company sees "how engagement in one sphere supports performance in the other.” The hope will be that, by allowing employees to play games, a productivity boost will follow.

Whether that comes to fruition remains to be seen. But there's less doubt about GTA 6's popularity a little more than a week out from its release. If you've yet to get your order in, you can also grab Grand Theft Auto VI for $79.99 now. You'll get a box with a code that you'll need to redeem on your PS5 to be able to download and play the game.

The game's release brings an end to years of rumors and leaks, not to mention legal battles. Take-Two hit Microsoft with a subpoena in relation to a massive leak earlier this year in an attempt to find the perpetrator. Rockstar Games addressed the leaks in a post on the X social network shortly after the subpoena was made public, saying that it "would be an understatement to say that having videos of Grand Theft Auto VI gameplay leak in this way has been heartbreaking for our team."

articles.title: Apple's touchscreen MacBook Pro does not like to be taken apart
articles.description: Easy lid swaps earn praise from iFixit, but panel removal ends in cracks and USB-C repairs require logic board surgery
articles.content:
Apple's first touchscreen MacBook got a mixed reception from iFixit's teardown specialists, who praised its easily replaced lid but found fans and USB-C ports buried beneath the logic board.

The MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR display was unveiled at the end of October. It features a tandem OLED screen that stacks two layers of organic light-emitting pixels, eliminating the need for a backlight, and adds touch capability to the MacBook line for the first time.

Although the vendor was patted on the back in recent years for improving the repairability of its famously locked-down products, this machine shows Apple still has some way to go.

The good? The entire lid comes off relatively easily. Its three-screw hinges closely resemble those on the M6 14-inch MacBook Pro, while streamlined display cable brackets simplify removal.

Apple's Repair Assistant tool also handled a full system board swap well. Despite concerns about Touch ID fingerprint authentication, everything went relatively smoothly when iFixit paired a touchscreen from one machine with a logic board from another. On the first boot, Repair Assistant recognized the battery, display, and Touch ID sensor, and touch control needed no separate calibration.

The bad? Replacing the panel alone is not possible. When iFixit tried to separate it from the lid, the glass delaminated, cracking the OLED and touch-sensitive layers beneath. That could make for a costlier repair than bargained for.

Under the bottom cover, the PROLED has a similar internal layout to the last few models of MacBook Pros, with the fans, board, speakers, and trackpad all in the same places.

That means the same annoyances persist. The MagSafe power connector can be removed via two screws and a bracket, yet the USB-C ports can't be extracted the same way because the logic board is in the way. The headphone jack and the fans also require removing the system board first, and the HDMI port and SDXC card reader are soldered to the board itself, as is the storage and memory.

Another gripe is that this MacBook's battery pack is hard to remove, though at least it is removable, unlike in many thin-and-light laptops. The tested Pro weighs 1.38 kg or about 3 pounds.

For these reasons, the MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR display earns a 5 out of 10 repairability score from iFixit, but this is actually a one point increase over the score it gave the M5 MacBook Pro.

The Apple logo has its own lighting. Older MacBooks with illuminated logos borrowed light from the LCD backlight shining through an apple-shaped window in the lid. This model uses a strip of LEDs along one edge of the logo, passing through a diffuser for an even glow. Because it sits behind the display panel, it would be nearly impossible to repair if it failed, especially if the panel is destroyed during removal.

Under a microscope, the PROLED XDR display looks very different from earlier MacBooks: the blue subpixel is significantly larger than the green and red ones.

The reason, we're told, is that blue OLED materials wear out faster, so a larger subpixel can emit the same amount of light while putting less strain on the material. ®

articles.title: Anorak secures $5M to let anyone create their own AI-powered games
articles.description: Anorak, a London-Chengdu entertainment tech company with the vision of “making any pursuit playable”, today announced a $5 million pre-seed round co-led by Play Ventures and Backed VC, with participat...
articles.content:
Anorak, a London-Chengdu entertainment tech company with the vision of “making any pursuit playable”, today announced a $5 million pre-seed round co-led by Play Ventures and Backed VC, with participation from Supercell and MTG.

Anorak is led by CEO Shaun Rutland, who co-founded Hutch – the mobile automotive games studio behind Top Drives and F1 Clash, acquired by MTG in 2020 – and Chief Creative Officer Jonathan Alpine, a founding employee at Hutch and its former Chief Creative Officer.  They are joined by co-founder Tak Fung, Chief of AI, who leads Anorak's AI lab in Chengdu, China.

The company, which began as a generative video research project, now has a 20-strong team across London and Chengdu, developing proprietary inference technology to make generative video faster, cheaper and more controllable, progressively enabling games and experiences to shift from pre-generated to generative, real-time interaction.

The company's medium is interactive generative video – generative video, made playable. Rather than simply prompting its way to new AI-bolstered versions of existing games, Anorak is building new play patterns from scratch, and the platform to go with them. It’s a platform where generated video responds to user choices and inputs in real time. The model pairs human creativity and playfulness with agentic ingenuity and visualisation to establish an entirely new entertainment medium; one that is playable, watchable, and shareable.

At Hutch, the team learned how deep a single subculture can run. Car enthusiasts didn't just play – they obsessed over details, built communities and held each game to their own standards. Anorak takes that lesson and applies it to every subculture there is: anglers, sneakerheads, padel players, birdwatchers, K-pop fans, and thousands of communities no publisher would ever greenlight a game for. 

Generative media changes the economics of serving these communities. Anorak will bring its interactive format to increasingly wider and specific interests, making entertainment viable for audiences that traditional game production economics have left underserved.

The aim is to hand those tools to real-world communities, so they can make playable content for themselves – shaped by their own in-jokes, rituals and taste, not a boardroom's guess at what a mass market wants. When anyone can make anything, Anorak believes taste becomes the scarce asset, and the communities that hold it should not only steer what is created, but become the creators.

Anorak is releasing new playable experiments on its blog  every week, with plans to launch a creator platform that will enable anyone to realise their ideas.

It won't be a traditional chatbot that turns a prompt into a game. Anorak believes creation should be as much fun as playing – it's about having fun making fun.

According to Shaun Rutland, CEO and co-founder, Anorak:

"Every time making got cheaper – in music, film and games – value moved to whoever had the taste to filter the flood. Generative is the biggest of those shifts yet, because almost anyone can now create. 
Anorak is about giving every community that power: real people making playable things for the people they actually care about."

According to Harri Manninen, Founding Partner, Play Ventures, Anorak is at the forefront of building a new form of interactive entertainment, turning generative video into experiences people can play, watch and share. 

“What makes the vision especially compelling is the opportunity not only to build for passionate communities, but to empower those communities to create entertainment around their own interests. 

Shaun, Jonathan and Tak combine a proven track record in entertainment with deep AI expertise, exactly the kind of team we want to back at the beginning of a new technology cycle.”

Alex Brunicki, Founding Partner, Backed VC, contends that most AI entertainment companies are using new tools to make old formats faster. 

“Anorak is asking a far more interesting question: what does entertainment look like when content is made by and for a community, especially if we shift away from the skeuomorphism that other companies are still approaching the space with?

Furthermore, the technical breakthroughs the team have made in the past 12 months make us extremely excited for what comes next with Anorak."

The funding will expand the London and Chengdu teams, bring the first playable formats to release, and establish the creator platform in early 2027.

articles.title: SpaceX develops its own ‘Kessel’ rack-scale system featuring 72 Nvidia Rubin GPUs for data centers in space, report claims
articles.description: SpaceX is reportedly developing a 'Kessel' rack-scale system design with 72 Nvidia Rubin GPUs that relies on a massive 84-layer PCB midplane.
articles.content:
SpaceX/xAI is developing a custom version of Nvidia's Vera Rubin NVL72 rack-scale AI system that replaces conventional NVLink cable assemblies with a massive 84-layer printed circuit board (PCB), in part for use in orbital data centers, reports SemiAnalysis. The system is codenamed Kessel and retains 36 Vera CPUs, 72 Rubin GPUs, and nine NVLink switch trays, but introduces a different solid-state interconnect architecture. While SpaceX/xAI will continue to buy Nvidia hardware directly from the company, Elon Musk's company will source other components independently, which could give it greater control over its hardware supply chain.

The Stout Owl: The ultimate Noctua G2 PC

The Kessel system retains the fundamental configuration of Nvidia's Vera Rubin NVL72 platform, which comprises 72 GPU packages distributed across 18 compute trays and nine NVLink switch trays. However, instead of Nvidia's conventional arrangement with internal NVLink cable cartridges, SpaceX plans to position compute and switch trays back-to-back around a passive PCB midplane. The architecture resembles a smaller version of Nvidia's Kyber design with 576 AI GPUs (albeit in 144 packages), which also relies on a PCB-based interconnect rather than conventional cable assemblies, SemiAnalysis notes. Interestingly, the design is aimed at both terrestrial and orbital deployments, according to the analysts.

Arguably the most distinctive feature of Kessel is its 84-layer PCB midplane, which uses ultra-low-loss M10 copper-clad laminates (CCLs). By contrast, Nvidia's Kyber architecture relied on a backplane based on a considerably more complex 156-layer PCB featuring M9 CCLs. The reduction in layer count by nearly half could substantially improve manufacturability and production yields, but the more advanced copper-clad laminate will almost certainly increase material costs. In any case, an 84-layer PCB is a device that is exceptionally hard to build.

The move to a PCB midplane could simplify system assembly by eliminating numerous high-speed cable connections, but it would not necessarily reduce manufacturing costs. An 84-layer PCB that relies on ultra-low-loss M10 laminate is an exceptionally expensive component that requires sophisticated manufacturing processes and precise quality control. To put an 84-layer PCB number into context, modern high-end server motherboards use 15 – 20 layers, whereas server development boards use more than 20 layers to virtually eliminate any electrical issues with the board itself. Furthermore, manufacturing yields of an 84-layer PCB could become a major obstacle, as defects in internal layers may render an entire board unusable. Consequently, the economic viability of Kessel will depend on whether savings from cable elimination and independent component procurement can offset the cost of its complex midplane.

Perhaps more importantly, Kessel represents a departure from Nvidia's conventional system-level procurement model. Instead of purchasing Nvidia's assembled L6 compute boards or even L10 trays that Nvidia plans to sell with its Vera Rubin generation, SpaceX reportedly plans to acquire AI accelerators, CPUs, switches, and networking components directly from Nvidia and procure other components from third-party suppliers (one can wonder how easy it will be for SpaceX/xAI to procure memory amid today's shortages). This would enable SpaceX to select its own PCB manufacturers, component vendors, and manufacturing partners, optimize its hardware for its infrastructure (which will be important for orbital deployments), and perhaps reduce intermediary costs. Meanwhile, the company would assume greater responsibility for system design, validation, manufacturing quality, and supply-chain management, which is something that most hyperscalers have been doing in recent years.

For Nvidia, the implications are less straightforward. Although direct sales of CPU and AI GPU packages could reduce the company's revenue from complete compute-board assemblies, the arrangement could also encourage other large customers to develop their own Nvidia-based systems and eventually deploy more Nvidia-based machines, something that may be important in a world where custom silicon developed by hyperscalers is rapidly gaining traction. However, to make this happen, Kessel must be a smashing success that will offer clear advantages over systems designed by Nvidia.

articles.title: CoreWeave tests AI integrations on its cloud before you migrate
articles.description: Moving an AI workload to another cloud means bringing more than a model and its data. Your serving layer, observability The post CoreWeave tests AI integrations on its cloud before you migrate appeared first on The New Stack .
articles.content:
Moving an AI workload to another cloud means bringing more than a model and its data. Your serving layer, observability dashboards, security controls, and storage systems have to work together on the new infrastructure. For platform teams, proving those connections under real traffic can become the slowest and riskiest part of the move.

As a stack grows across vendors and clouds, each project adds more integration questions. A compatible specification is a starting point. It doesn’t guarantee a tool will behave as expected in production, or that the runbooks and security workflows built around it will carry over.

Make production validation visible

An integration needs to work on the infrastructure where you plan to run it, under production traffic. The tools should also be ones your team already uses or has asked for.

“A compatible specification is a starting point. It doesn’t guarantee a tool will behave as expected in production, or that the runbooks and security workflows built around it will carry over.”

We built the CoreWeave Partner Network to make that validation visible. It brings relationships with CrowdStrike, VAST Data, Reflection, IBM, and other technology vendors into a curated network of integrations tested under real-world production conditions on CoreWeave Cloud.

The network covers four parts of the AI stack, from training and inference to data movement, security, and the next iteration:

Infrastructure: compute, storage, networking, servers, and interconnects, with partners including VAST Data, Dell, AMD, IBM, BackBlaze, and Pulumi.

Data services: storing, processing, moving, and accessing AI data throughout its lifecycle, with ClickHouse, Encord, LanceDB, and Datology.

Independent software vendors (ISVs): orchestration, observability, and model development, including Grafana, Datadog, Union, SkyPilot, IBM, Pinecone, Redis, LlamaIndex, and Clockwork. A dedicated security segment includes CrowdStrike, Zscaler, and Cranium.

Models, agents, and inference: foundational software and services for building, training, serving, and scaling applications, with Reflection, RadixArk, Inferact, OpenRouter, and Red Hat.

Together, these integrations support running and observing models, curating data, improving behavior, and evaluating the next release. Every partner must meet the same requirement: an integration that works on CoreWeave infrastructure under production conditions. Partners enter the network because customers run them or ask for them.

Read the workload evidence

IBM trained its Granite models on CoreWeave around one of the first deployments of Nvidia GB200 NVL72 clusters. Cohere built North, its agentic AI platform, on one of the industry’s first production GB200 NVL72 clusters and reported training three times faster than on Nvidia Hopper.

Mistral AI trains its models entirely on CoreWeave and cites training 2.5 times faster on Nvidia GB200 NVL72 systems. Decart uses Nvidia HGX B200 at production scale through its CoreWeave collaboration, on a platform that includes Weights & Biases.

The underlying relationships predate the network announcement. CoreWeave and Weights & Biases have run production integrations with Encord, Pinecone, and other partners since the early wave of open-source large language models (LLMs) and frontier-model training.

Jon Jones, CoreWeave’s Chief Revenue Officer, describes the change as making existing partner work visible before customers build. The network also provides a repeatable way to pursue deeper integrations, joint go-to-market work, and shared innovation.

The partners emphasize different parts of that system. VAST Data co-founder and chief technology officer Alon Horev describes combining CoreWeave’s AI cloud with the VAST AI Operating System across large-scale training, fine-tuning, production inference, and continuous agentic workloads. CrowdStrike CEO and founder George Kurtz emphasizes security built into the infrastructure running AI. Adam Lawrence, general manager of IBM Americas, points to IBM and Red Hat technologies as a way to expand choice and reduce integration work when deploying and scaling AI.

Carry over the operations you already use

Your team has already built runbooks around its observability tools. Grafana and Datadog integrations let you carry that work over. CrowdStrike, Zscaler, and Cranium provide security integrations, bringing existing threat visibility and response tooling.

Inference integrations serve a similar purpose: keeping the models available as teams expand onto CoreWeave, without rebuilding the serving layer. The goal is to add capacity while retaining the parts of the stack that already work.

“A marketplace listing still leaves your team to validate the integration. An LLM can suggest what’s popular without telling you what works on your infrastructure.”

A marketplace listing still leaves your team to validate the integration. An LLM can suggest what’s popular without telling you what works on your infrastructure. We select partners based on customer demand and test their integrations across all four segments.

Include the tools your agents call

The integration problem also reaches inside agent execution. Most closed models include web search, while most open-weight models do not. Teams choosing open weights for cost, control, or customization have often had to connect a search provider separately.

CoreWeave is extending its partner approach to these tools, beginning with Exa, Parallel Web Systems, and You.com. The announced search layer provides access through one integration instead of a separate contract for each provider.

Teams can enable it through a single setting on a standard inference request or access it from inside a CoreWeave Sandbox, without setting up a separate software development kit (SDK) or account. The arrangement is nonexclusive, so using the integration does not restrict future provider choices.

We announced the search partnerships at Fully Connected, with the remaining integration work planned for the following weeks. As those integrations become available, they will meet the same production-validation standard as the rest of the network.

Start with the connections your workload needs

Before adding another cloud, check the serving, data, observability, and security connections your workload depends on. Ask which integrations have been tested under production conditions and what your team will still need to validate.

“Before adding another cloud, check the serving, data, observability, and security connections your workload depends on.”

The CoreWeave Partner Network lists validated partners. CoreWeave account teams can discuss a specific integration and workload, and partner sessions from Fully Connected 2026 offer another way to see the integrations in use. Teams interested in new collaborations can explore the partner program.

articles.title: Microsoft's Patch Tuesday can't break stuff if it won't install
articles.description: KB5132061 throws 0x800F0993 and 0x800F0989 errors, and Redmond is saying nothing
articles.content:
Users are having difficulty installing Microsoft's latest Windows patch.

Patch Tuesday contained a truckload of fixes for Microsoft products. However, for some users, installing the update, KB5132061, is proving challenging. In the hours after the patch was released, multiple complaints began to surface that the download and installation were failing, with some customers reporting a 0x800F0993 error code. Others say they received a 0x800F0989 error.

Microsoft does not currently list any known issues with the update and is yet to make a statement or provide explanation for the glitch.

In addition to the security fixes, this patch resolves a number of known issues from previous updates, including a problem where USB Audio 1.0 devices might fail to start and display an error code 10 in Device Manager.

In the absence of a statement from Microsoft, several users have taken to sleuthing. One, with the handle of Forceflow on the ElevenForum site, suggested the bug might be related to Windows Sandbox, and said that after disabling the feature and rebooting, the patch installed successfully.

However, others reported problems regardless of Windows Sandbox status, and alternative solutions included using DISM (Deployment Image Servicing and Management) to check the package or downloading the update manually.

It's an important patch to install, since it addresses 726 vulnerabilities in Windows alone, and the difficulties affected users face are less than ideal.

Microsoft patches have lately displayed more gremlins than usual. Out-of-band releases are depressingly regular after updates break functionality. A September Out-of-band release, for example, was hurriedly pushed out after the September 2026 Windows security update caused trouble for Remote Desktop Services.

The October Patch Tuesday for Windows Server sent Exchange Servers toppling, with a registry edit workaround suggested. There was no out-of-band update - Microsoft said the problem had been resolved in the November update.

At least this latest release appears to be failing before users get a chance to see what is broken this time. ®

Updated to add on November 12:

Microsoft has confirmed that there was indeed a problem with installing the update for some users, but the good news is that a fix is rolling out and no action is required on the part of customers (at least those connected to the internet and using Windows Update).

The bad news is, alas, there appear to be a few issues with the update around printing and activation. Microsoft giveth, and Microsoft taketh away.

articles.title: Softbank loses $3.7 billion on canceled AI data center gas turbine orders days after denying Elon Musk’s claim it was defaulting
articles.description: SoftBank might not have defaulted on a raft of gas turbine orders, but it has pulled out of deals for unwanted power units after overestimating how many it could use amid the AI data center buildout boom.
articles.content:
By early 2026, Japanese tech investment outfit SoftBank had reserved more power generation capacity than the entire state of Connecticut after cornering a huge portion of the global gas turbine production capacity. Now, the same company has chosen to take a $3.7 billion hit to its earnings after canceling reservations for the highly sought-after power generation hardware. The WSJ reports that SoftBank had reserved more than 13 gigawatts of power-producing turbines, citing unnamed "people familiar with the orders." That's the equivalent of more than six Hoover Dams' worth of capacity, with SoftBank founder and chief executive Masayoshi Son believing that it would be vital to the company's earning potential moving forward. Notably, this development surfaced after SoftBank's CFO fired back at Elon Musk's recent revelation that the company had defaulted on turbine blade contracts, saying, "there is no such default."

(Image credit: Microsoft) The data center cooling state of play

Demand for data center CPUs has surged, and AI agents are responsible

The gas turbines were to power AI data centers, and SoftBank is set to build a 9.2-gigawatt power plant in Ohio, with construction scheduled for early 2027. It'll cost $33 billion to build and will provide power to a neighboring eight-gigawatt data center. That data center will be leased to OpenAI, albeit only after Nvidia entered discussions about guaranteeing around $250 billion of financing for the project.

But SoftBank got ahead of itself. After initially planning to use the turbines for future gas-powered plants, the company has now chosen to change direction. Orders for turbines, engines that convert natural gas into the electricity used by data centers, must be placed years in advance of them being required. The company had bet big, placing huge orders with the expectation that demand would greatly outstrip supply. That would leave SoftBank in an enviable position, holding huge orders for the vital components required as part of a data center rollout boosted by AI demand. But those reservations weren't cheap — turbine manufacturers regularly charge customers tens of millions of dollars per gigawatt.

It's now canceled its remaining reservations with GE Vernova, its turbine supplier, while also unwinding contracts for orders that were too far gone. SoftBank told investors on a recent earnings call that the orders had been placed “to secure power generation equipment in anticipation of shortages,” but it now appears it anticipated a little too much.

Crucially, SoftBank is also keen for everyone to know that this move was voluntary and that it did not default on its orders. That's contrary to what xAI CEO Elon Musk claimed in a post on his X social network. SoftBank Chief Financial Officer Yoshimitsu Goto was quick to counter Musk's claims. “This is simply not correct at all,” Goto reportedly said. “There is no such default.”

US big-hitting VCs Lightspeed and Alphabet's CapitalG have backed UK chip startup  Fractile in a £500m-plus funding round, which values the startup at over £5bn, the UK government said today in a press release.

The UK Nvidia challenger, based in Bristol and London, designs chips for AI inference, the process of running an AI model.

Founded in 2022 by Oxford PhD Walter Goodwin, Fractile’s architecture keeps data directly on the chip, unlike standard chips that must constantly shuttle data between the processor and separate memory modules.
It says this method can run LLMs up to a hundred times faster than existing hardware while lowering operational costs by 90 per cent. Fractile's specialised chips are set to be ready for data centre deployment next year.

The lead investors in the Series C round, some of which has previously been reported, are Thrive Capital, Peter Thiel's Founders Fund, Lightspeed, and Redpoint. The UK’s Sovereign AI fund, the British Business Bank, Shopify, Balderton, Dragoneer and Blackrock also featured in the round, which Fractile said amounted to around £540m.

It follows its $220m Series B, which it announced in May this year, led by Accel, Factorial Funds, and Founders Fund. The Series B funding round valued Fractile at around £820m.

The investment comes as the UK looks to become a leader in parts of the AI stack and build up its sovereign capabilities in critical technologies, reducing dependence on fragile overseas supply chains.

AI minister Kanishka Narayan said: “For too long, Britain has produced some of the world’s best scientific ideas, only to see too much of the technology, industry and wealth they create built elsewhere.
We are determined to change that. If AI is going to serve the British people, strengthen our public services and create good jobs across the country, Britain needs to build more of the technology that powers it.

“Fractile represents the very best of British ambition, bringing together world-class chip design, engineering and AI expertise to develop faster, cheaper and more energy-efficient hardware.”

articles.title: NASA asks Earthlings to wave as Voyager 1 reaches a light-day away
articles.description: Flash VGR in Morse code on November 17 to salute the veteran probe – just don't expect it to see you
articles.content:
Voyager 1 will become the first human-made object to reach one light-day from Earth next week, and NASA wants us to mark the occasion by flashing our lights at the sky.

The spacecraft, which suffered a communications hiccup last month, is traveling at approximately 38,000 mph (61,000 kph) and will mark the 50th anniversary of its launch next year. Before then, it has another distance record to set.

"Light-day" is a bit snappier than 16,094,799,096 miles (25,902,068,356 kilometers). NASA puts the crossing at 05:16:07 EST (10:16:07 UTC) on Wednesday, November 18.

For "Shine Bright for Voyager's Light-Day," participants are invited to flash the mission's three-letter designation – VGR – in Morse code after sunset on November 17, using a flashlight or NASA's website.

According to the space agency, this will create "a symbolic wave of golden light encircling the planet after sunset." It is also a nice way to mark the achievement – Voyager 1 is the most distant human-made object from Earth, and its extraordinary longevity remains a testament to the skill of engineers past and present.

Not that Voyager 1 will be able to detect any flashlights on Earth. Its cameras were turned off decades ago, after the famous Pale Blue Dot image was captured.

NASA has invited the public to join in a spacecraft photo opportunity before. On July 19, 2013, Cassini photographed Earth and the Moon from its orbit around Saturn for "The Day the Earth Smiled," while people back home were encouraged to look up and "just smile at the sheer joy of being alive on a Pale Blue Dot."

Voyager 2, the spacecraft's sibling, is not expected to reach the same milestone for another nine years. It took a different path through the solar system to swing past Uranus and Neptune.

It will, however, be uncertain as to whether Voyager 2 will still be able to communicate by then – even with recent efforts to eke out the probe's dwindling power supply, margins are razor thin. ®
